Since a proof stands for its theorem, these definitional \ref edges closed result cycles (TP2 -> LP2 -> LP3 -> TP2). The rules give no case for this, so I marked those edges, and the step-level 'as in Theorem 2.2' refs, as mention: true. The cycle comes from layout; the argument is not circular.

Appendix equations (A.2) and (A.4) are cited results of Strasser (Lemma 55.4, Corollary 59.6), so I retyped them as external theorems rather than equations. The Le Cam distance equation (A.3) stays inside a definition.

These are roadmap paragraphs that open Sections 4 and 5. I could have made them part of the proofs, but they contain no argument, so I typed them as remarks and gave them mention edges to the results they announce.

The proofs of Theorems 2.1 and 2.2 run as prose across subsections, with the auxiliary lemmas stated and proved in between. I emitted one proof node per part, each with a proves edge, and gave the continuation a uses edge to the first part.

Section 2.3 gives Monte Carlo evidence (Tables 1-3: likelihood-ratio quantiles and Wilcoxon tests). I captured only the verbal conclusion, as a claim with rigor numerical. The tables themselves are not nodes.

Not extracted: the introduction and conclusion summaries, the discussion of practical volatility estimation in Section 2.4 (Hubalek-Posedel and others), the description of the simulation design, and the interpretive sentence after the epsilon-deficiency definition in the Appendix.

The source has small notational slips. Part I of the proof of Theorem 2.2 cites N_n 'as in (defNn)', but that equation defines N_{1,n}. Part II of the proof of Theorem 2.1 writes theta=(h_0,beta,alpha,gamma). Statements are copied verbatim.

nodes.name: Randomly thinned innovations $Z_n$
nodes.statement: For all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ we consider an $n$-dimensional vector $Z_{n}=(Z_{n,k})_{1\le k\le n}$ with distribution \begin{equation} {\mathcal L}(Z_n) = \bigl((1 - p_n)\varepsilon_0+p_n Q_n \bigr)^{\otimes n} , \end{equation} where, for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $p_n\in(0,1)$ and $Q_n$ is a probability measure on the Borel field ${\mathcal B}(\mathbb{R})$. Here, $\epsilon_0$ denotes the Dirac measure with total mass in zero.
nodes.section: GARCH-type experiments in discrete and continuous time
nodes.statement_short: $Z_n$ has i.i.d. components equal to 0 w.p. $1-p_n$ and drawn from $Q_n$ w.p. $p_n$.

nodes.name: Law of the thinned innovation vector

nodes.name: Law of rare events
nodes.statement: In accordance with the law of rare events, we assume that the following limit exists in $(0,\infty)$: \begin{equation} \gamma = \lim_{n\to\infty}np_n\in (0,\infty) . \end{equation}
nodes.section: GARCH-type experiments in discrete and continuous time
nodes.statement_short: The thinning probabilities satisfy $np_n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$.

nodes.name: Rare-events limit $\gamma=\lim np_n$
nodes.statement: \gamma = \lim_{n\to\infty}np_n\in (0,\infty) .

nodes.label: lre

nodes.name: Parametrization
nodes.statement: Throughout this paper, a parametrization is a pair $(\Theta,(H_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}),$ where $\Theta$ is a non-empty subset of $[0,\infty)^4,$ and for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $H_n$ is a mapping $H_n=(h_{0,n},\beta_n,\alpha_n,\lambda_n)\dvtx\Theta\to[0,\infty)^4$.
nodes.section: GARCH-type experiments in discrete and continuous time

nodes.name: Randomly thinned GARCH
nodes.statement: For a parametrization $(\Theta,(H_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}),$ we consider the sequence of partial sums corresponding to a \textit{randomly thinned} GARCH model indexed by $\theta\in\Theta$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$, defined by \begin{eqnarray} G_{n}(k)&=&G_{n}(k - 1)+h^{1/2}_n(k - 1) Z_{n,k} ,\qquad G_n(0) = 0 ,\nonumber\\ h_{n}(k)&=&\beta_n(\theta)+\alpha_n(\theta) h_{n}(k - 1)+ \lambda_n(\theta) h_{n}(k - 1) Z_{n,k}^2 ,\\ h_{n}(0)&=&h_{0,n}(\theta),\qquad 1\le k\le n ,\ \theta\in\Theta,\nonumber \end{eqnarray} where $H_n(\theta)=(h_{0,n}(\theta),\beta_n(\theta),\alpha_n(\theta ),\lambda_n(\theta))$ for all $\theta\in\Theta$.
nodes.section: GARCH-type experiments in discrete and continuous time
nodes.statement_short: GARCH partial sums $G_n$ with volatility recursion $h_n$ driven by thinned innovations $Z_{n,k}$.

nodes.name: Randomly thinned GARCH recursion
nodes.statement: G_{n}(k)&=&G_{n}(k - 1)+h^{1/2}_n(k - 1) Z_{n,k} ,\qquad G_n(0) = 0 ,\nonumber\\ h_{n}(k)&=&\beta_n(\theta)+\alpha_n(\theta) h_{n}(k - 1)+ \lambda_n(\theta) h_{n}(k - 1) Z_{n,k}^2 ,\\ h_{n}(0)&=&h_{0,n}(\theta),\qquad 1\le k\le n ,\ \theta\in\Theta,\nonumber
nodes.section: GARCH-type experiments in discrete and continuous time
nodes.label: G1

nodes.name: COGARCH
nodes.statement: COGARCH is a process $(G,h)=(G(t),h(t))_{0\le t\le1}$ that is indexed by $\theta=(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in[0,\infty)^4$ and determined as the unique pathwise solution of the following system of integral equations: \begin{eqnarray} G(t)&=&\int_{[0,t]\times\mathbb{R}} h^{1/2}(s-)z N(\mathrm{d}s,\mathrm{d}z) ,\nonumber\\ [-8pt]\\ [-8pt] h(t)&=&h_0+ \int_{[0,t]} \beta - \alpha h(s-)\,\mathrm{d}s+\lambda \int_{[0,t]\times\mathbb{R}} h(s-)z^2 N(\mathrm{d}s,\mathrm{d}z),\nonumber \end{eqnarray} where $N$ is a Poisson point measure on $[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}$ with intensity $\gamma\ell\otimes Q$.
nodes.section: GARCH-type experiments in discrete and continuous time
nodes.statement_short: COGARCH driven by a compound Poisson point measure $N$, as the pathwise solution of jump integral equations for $(G,h)$.

nodes.name: COGARCH integral equations

nodes.name: Random time change $T_\sigma$
nodes.statement: Here, $T\dvtx\mathbb{M}_1\to D_1$, $\sigma\mapsto T_\sigma$ is defined as follows: If, for some $m\in\mathbb{N}$, $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_{m}< 1$ and $x_1,\dots,x_m\in \mathbb{R}$, $\sigma\in\mathbb{M}$ admits a representation of the form $\sigma=\sum_{k=1}^m\varepsilon_{(t_k,x_k)}$, where $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_{m}< 1$, then we set \begin{eqnarray} T_{\sigma}(t)&=& \frac{t - t_k}{m(t_k - t_{k - 1})}+\frac km ,\qquad t\in [t_{k-1},t_k), 1\le k\le m ,\nonumber\\ [-9pt]\\ [-9pt] T_{\sigma}(t)&=&\frac{t - t_m}{m(t_m - t_{m - 1})}+1,\qquad t\in[t_{m},1].\nonumber \end{eqnarray} If such a representation does not exist, then we set $T_{\sigma}(t)=t$ for all $t\in[0,1]$.

nodes.statement: Let (\ref{lre}) be satisfied for some $\gamma\in(0,\infty)$ and $p_n\in(0,1)$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Maller 	extit{et al.} \cite{MMS08} have encountered a slightly different scenario. For $	heta\in\Theta,$ they have embedded a sequence of GARCH models into a given COGARCH and obtained the convergence with respect to the same topology, now driven by a general L'{e}vy process, even in probability. If the driving process is a compound Poisson process with rate $\gamma$ and jump size distribution $Q$, then their analysis relates to a situation where the corresponding partial sums have the same law as $(G_n[n\cdot],h_n[n\cdot])$ under the parametrization $H^{\mathrm{(M)}}_n(	heta)$, $	heta\in\Theta$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$. In short, it follows from the analyses in \cite{KV07} that, for fixed $	heta\in\Theta$, the partial sum processes of GARCH with parametrization $H^{(KV)}_n(	heta)$ converge to COGARCH in law, as $n	o\infty$, with a similar result being true for the parametrization $H^{(M)}_n(	heta)$ in~\cite{MMS08}. On the other hand, both parametrizations fall into the framework of Theorem ef{th2a}. Hence, if the distribution of the innovations admits a Lebesgue density, then the limiting experiment is given by MCOGARCH $\widehat {\mathcal E}(\Theta)$ rather than COGARCH ${\mathcal E}(\Theta)$.\vadjust{\goodbreak} (ii) In part (i), $Q=Q_n$ does not depend on $n$. Potential applications where $Q_n$ depends on~$n$ arise in the peak-over-threshold method in extreme value theory; see, for instance, Embrechts 	extit{et al.} \cite{EK97}, Resnick \cite{Re87} and Falk 	extit{et al.} \cite{FHR00}. Also, the corresponding GARCH models converge in distribution in law to a COGARCH driven by a compound Poisson process with jump distribution $Q$. On the other hand, if $Q_n$ converges to $Q$, even in total variation norm, then it follows from Theorem ef{th2} that the corresponding limiting experiment must be statistically equivalent to MCOGARCH.

nodes.name: Function $g_{f,\zeta}$
nodes.statement: Let $f\dvtx\mathbb{R}\to(0,\infty]$ be a strictly positive probability density with respect to Lebesgue measure and set \begin{equation} g_{f, \zeta}(h):=h^\zeta \int_\mathbb{R} f(hz)^\zeta f(z)^{1-\zeta}\,\mathrm{d}z,\qquad h>0 , \zeta\in(0,1). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Theorem 2.3 (COGARCH vs. MCOGARCH non-equivalence)
nodes.statement: Let $\varnothing\neq\Theta\subseteq (0,\infty)\times[0,\infty)^3$. Assume that $Q$ admits a strictly positive Lebesgue density $f$ such that for some $\zeta_0\in(0,1)$, $g_{f, \zeta_0}\dvtx(0,\infty)\to[0,1]$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1]$. Let $(\gamma_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be a sequence such that $\gamma=\lim_{n\to\infty} \gamma_n$ exists in $[0,\infty)$ and $\gamma_n\neq\gamma$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$. If ${\mathcal E}_{\gamma_n,Q}(\Theta)$ is equivalent to $\widehat{\mathcal E}_{\gamma_n,Q}(\Theta)$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N},$ then we have: \begin{longlist} \item if $(h_{0,1},\beta,\alpha,\lambda),(h_{0,2},\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in \Theta$ and $\beta>0$, then $h_{0,1}= h_{0,2}$; \item if $(h_{0},\beta_1,\alpha,\lambda),(h_{0},\beta_2,\alpha,\lambda)\in \Theta$, then $\beta_{1}= \beta_{2}$; \item if $(h_{0},\beta,\alpha_1,\lambda),(h_{0},\beta,\alpha_2,\lambda)\in \Theta$ and $\beta=0$, then $\alpha_1=\alpha_{2}$;\vadjust{\goodbreak} \item if $(h_{0},\beta,\alpha_1,\lambda),(h_{0},\beta,\alpha_2,\lambda)\in \Theta$ and $\alpha_1=0$, then $\alpha_{2}=0$; \item if $(h_{0},\beta,\alpha_1,\lambda),(h_{0},\beta,\alpha_2,\lambda)\in \Theta$ and $\alpha_1<\alpha_2$, then $h_0>\beta/\alpha_{1}$. \end{longlist}
assumptions: Let $\varnothing\neq\Theta\subseteq (0,\infty)\times[0,\infty)^3$.
Assume that $Q$ admits a strictly positive Lebesgue density $f$ such that for some $\zeta_0\in(0,1)$, $g_{f, \zeta_0}\dvtx(0,\infty)\to[0,1]$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1]$.
Let $(\gamma_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be a sequence such that $\gamma=\lim_{n\to\infty} \gamma_n$ exists in $[0,\infty)$ and $\gamma_n\neq\gamma$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$.
If ${\mathcal E}_{\gamma_n,Q}(\Theta)$ is equivalent to $\widehat{\mathcal E}_{\gamma_n,Q}(\Theta)$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N},$
nodes.statement_short: If COGARCH and MCOGARCH experiments are equivalent along intensities $\gamma_n\to\gamma$, the parameter set must be degenerate (lower-dimensional).
nodes.label: th1

nodes.name: Equivalence restricted to lower-dimensional parameter sets
nodes.statement: Theorem 2.3 indicates that equivalence of MCOGARCH and COGARCH is restricted to parameter sets that are of considerably lower dimension and which have non-empty interiors. Hence, we do not have equivalence in deficiency.

nodes.name: $g_{f,\zeta}$ as a Hellinger transformation
nodes.statement: Observe that $\zeta\mapsto g_{f,\zeta}(h)$ occurs as the Hellinger transformation of the scaling experiment $(\mathbb{R},{\mathcal B}(\mathbb{R}),\{{\mathcal L}(Z),{\mathcal L}(Z/h)\})$, where $Z$ is a random variable with Lebesgue density $f$.

nodes.name: Generalized symmetric gamma distribution
nodes.statement: \textit{Generalized symmetric gamma distribution.} Let $a,b,c>0$ and $\Gamma$ be Euler's gamma function. Assume that $f\dvtx\mathbb{R}\to(0,\infty]$ has the following form: \[ f(z) = \frac12 \frac{a^{c/b}}{\Gamma(c/b)} \mathrm{e}^{-a|z|^b}|z|^{c-1},\qquad z\in\mathbb{R} . \] This class of distributions covers important special cases such as the normal distribution with zero mean and the Laplace distribution. It follows straightforwardly that \[ g_{f, \zeta}(h) = \biggl(\frac{h^{b\zeta}}{h^b\zeta+(1-\zeta )} \biggr)^{c/b},\qquad 0<\zeta<1,\ h>0 . \] Observe that $g_{f,\zeta}\dvtx(0,\infty)\to[0,1]$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1]$ for all $0 < \zeta < 1$ and thus~$f$ satisfies the monotonicity assumption of Theorem \ref{th1}.
nodes.statement_short: For generalized symmetric gamma densities (incl. normal, Laplace), $g_{f,\zeta}$ is explicit and strictly increasing on $(0,1]$.

nodes.name: Centered Cauchy distribution
nodes.statement: \textit{Centered Cauchy distribution.} Let $a>0$ and $f_a(z)= \frac a{\uppi}\frac1{1+(az)^2}$ be the density of the centered $\operatorname{Cauchy}$ distribution $\operatorname{Cauchy}(0,a)$ with scaling parameter $a$. By the scaling property in (\ref{gfzscalingrefl}), we have $g_{f_a, 1/2}(h)=g_{f_1, 1/2}(h)$ for all $h>0$. By differentiating this under the integral sign, we obtain \[ \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}h}g_{f_a, 1/2}(h)=\frac{1 - h^2}{2\uppi h^2} \int _0^\infty \frac{\sqrt{x}\,\mathrm{d}x}{(1+(1+h^2)x/h+x^2)^{3/2}}>0,\qquad a>0 , 0<h\le1 . \] Consequently, the centered $\operatorname{Cauchy}$ distribution satisfies the monotonicity assumption of Theorem \ref{th1}.
nodes.statement_short: For centered Cauchy densities, differentiating $g_{f,1/2}$ shows it is strictly increasing on $(0,1]$.

nodes.name: Equivalence via equal likelihood-ratio laws (Strasser, Theorem 53.10)
nodes.statement: Recall that statistical equivalence of the experiments ${\mathcal E}$ and $\widehat{\mathcal E}$ is implied (see \cite{St85}, Theorem 53.10) when, for all finite subsets $\Theta\subseteq[0,\infty)^4$ and all $\theta_0\in\Theta$, we have \begin{equation} {\mathcal L}_{\theta_0} \biggl( \biggl(\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathcal L}_{\theta}(G)}{\mathrm{d}{\mathcal L} _{\theta_0}(G)} \biggr)_{\theta\in\Theta} \biggr) = {\mathcal L}_{\theta_0} \biggl( \biggl(\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathcal L}_{\theta}(\widehat G)}{\mathrm{d}{\mathcal L}_{\theta_0}(\widehat G)} \biggr)_{\theta\in\Theta} \biggr). \end{equation}
assumptions: for all finite subsets $\Theta\subseteq[0,\infty)^4$ and all $\theta_0\in\Theta$, we have
conclusions: statistical equivalence of the experiments ${\mathcal E}$ and $\widehat{\mathcal E}$ is implied

nodes.name: Equality of likelihood-ratio laws
nodes.statement: {\mathcal L}_{\theta_0} \biggl( \biggl(\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathcal L}_{\theta}(G)}{\mathrm{d}{\mathcal L} _{\theta_0}(G)} \biggr)_{\theta\in\Theta} \biggr) = {\mathcal L}_{\theta_0} \biggl( \biggl(\frac{\mathrm{d}{\mathcal L}_{\theta}(\widehat G)}{\mathrm{d}{\mathcal L}_{\theta_0}(\widehat G)} \biggr)_{\theta\in\Theta} \biggr).
nodes.label: COGMCOGdis

nodes.name: Simulation evidence of non-equivalence
nodes.statement: Based on $10^6$ samples, the null hypothesis is most significantly rejected, for all three jump distributions and all eight parameter vectors $\theta_{ij}$. In other words, there is strong evidence that in the case of incomplete observations, the randomly thinned GARCH and COGARCH experiments are not statistically equivalent for these jump distributions.
conclusions: in the case of incomplete observations, the randomly thinned GARCH and COGARCH experiments are not statistically equivalent for these jump distributions
nodes.statement_short: Wilcoxon tests on $10^6$ simulated likelihood ratios reject equality for all three jump laws and all eight parameter pairs.

nodes.name: Non-equivalence for arbitrary jump distributions
nodes.statement: This confirms our conjecture, that Theorem \ref{th1} holds in a much more general formulation for quite arbitrary jump distributions.
conclusions: Theorem \ref{th1} holds in a much more general formulation for quite arbitrary jump distributions

nodes.name: Fully observed experiments ${\mathcal E}_h$, $\widehat{\mathcal E}_h$
nodes.statement: Returning to theoretical matters, we now consider the following GARCH-type experiments in continuous time with fully observed volatilities, denoted by \[ {\mathcal E}_h= \bigl(D_2,{\mathcal D}_2, ({\mathcal L}_{\theta}(G,h) )_{\theta\in [0,\infty)^4} \bigr),\qquad \widehat{\mathcal E}_h= \bigl(D_2,{\mathcal D}_2, ({\mathcal L}_{\theta}(\widehat G,\hat h) )_{\theta\in[0,\infty)^4} \bigr) , \] where $\hat h$ is defined by the specification in (\ref{hatEEE}) and (\ref{timechange}).

nodes.name: Exceptional points $\Theta_e$
nodes.statement: We need to specify a set $\Theta_{e}\subseteq[0,\infty)^4$ of {\em exceptional points} in the parameter space $[0,\infty)^4$ as follows: \begin{equation} \Theta_{e} = \{\theta=(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in[0,\infty )^4\dvtx h_0\alpha=\beta\} . \end{equation}

nodes.name: Set of exceptional points
nodes.statement: \Theta_{e} = \{\theta=(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in[0,\infty )^4\dvtx h_0\alpha=\beta\} .
nodes.label: defThetae

nodes.name: Exceptional points and the volatility fixed point
nodes.statement: Observe that $\Theta_e$ is closely connected to the fixed point of the affine differential equation $h'(t)=\beta-\alpha h(t)$. Indeed, if $\theta=(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in\Theta_{e}$, then we have $h(t)=\hat h(t)\equiv h_0$ for all $t\in[0,T)$, where $T$ is the first jump of (M)COGARCH. It is impossible to recover the parameters $\beta,\alpha,\lambda$ in full within the time horizon $[0,T)$. Otherwise, if $h_0$ is not the fixed point of this differential equation, then it is always possible to recover parts of $\theta$ by taking appropriate derivatives.
nodes.statement_short: At exceptional points the volatility stays at its fixed point until the first jump, so $\beta,\alpha,\lambda$ cannot be recovered from that stretch.

nodes.name: Proposition 2.1 (reference experiment ${\mathcal F}$)
nodes.statement: If $Q(\{0\})=0,$ then both ${\mathcal E}_h$ and $\widehat{\mathcal E}_h$ are equivalent to ${\mathcal F}= ([0,\infty]^4,{\mathcal B}([0,\break\infty]^4),(Q_{\theta})_{\theta \in[0,\infty)^4} )$ where, for $\theta=(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in[0,\infty)^4$, $\gamma>0$, we set\vspace*{-2pt} \begin{equation} Q_{\theta} = \cases{ \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma} \varepsilon_{(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\infty)} + (1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}) \varepsilon_{\theta},&\quad $\theta\notin\Theta_{e}$,\cr \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma} \varepsilon_{(h_{0},\infty,\infty,\infty)} + (1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}) \varepsilon_{\theta} ,&\quad $\theta\in\Theta_{e} , h_0 > 0,\lambda > 0$,\cr \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma} \varepsilon_{(h_{0},\infty,\infty,\infty)} + (1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}) \varepsilon_{(h_{0},\infty,\infty,0)} ,&\quad $\theta\in\Theta_{e}, h_0 > 0 , \lambda = 0$,\cr \varepsilon_{(0,\infty,\infty,\infty)} ,&\quad $\theta\in\Theta_{e}, h_0 = 0$, }\vspace*{-2pt} \end{equation} and $\Theta_e$ is the set defined as in (\ref{defThetae}).\vspace*{-2pt}
conclusions: both ${\mathcal E}_h$ and $\widehat{\mathcal E}_h$ are equivalent to ${\mathcal F}= ([0,\infty]^4,{\mathcal B}([0,\break\infty]^4),(Q_{\theta})_{\theta \in[0,\infty)^4} )$
nodes.statement_short: With observed volatilities, COGARCH and MCOGARCH are both equivalent to a simple four-dimensional reference experiment ${\mathcal F}$.
nodes.label: prop1

nodes.name: Reference distributions $Q_\theta$
nodes.statement: Q_{\theta} = \cases{ \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma} \varepsilon_{(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\infty)} + (1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}) \varepsilon_{\theta},&\quad $\theta\notin\Theta_{e}$,\cr \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma} \varepsilon_{(h_{0},\infty,\infty,\infty)} + (1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}) \varepsilon_{\theta} ,&\quad $\theta\in\Theta_{e} , h_0 > 0,\lambda > 0$,\cr \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma} \varepsilon_{(h_{0},\infty,\infty,\infty)} + (1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}) \varepsilon_{(h_{0},\infty,\infty,0)} ,&\quad $\theta\in\Theta_{e}, h_0 > 0 , \lambda = 0$,\cr \varepsilon_{(0,\infty,\infty,\infty)} ,&\quad $\theta\in\Theta_{e}, h_0 = 0$, }\vspace*{-2pt}
nodes.label: defhatQthetan

nodes.name: Remark 2.2 (atoms of $Q$ at zero)
nodes.statement: In the situation of Proposition \ref {prop1}, we require $Q$ to satisfy $Q(\{0\})=0$. Indeed, if $Q=\varepsilon_0$, then it is easy to see that both ${\mathcal E}_h$ and $\widehat{\mathcal E}_h$ are equivalent to ${\mathcal F}$, where we formally set $\gamma=0$ in (\ref{defhatQthetan}). Otherwise, if $Q(\{0\})\in[0,1)$, then we may \vspace{1pt} adjust the intensity measures of the driving Poisson measure accordingly, to see that both ${\mathcal E}_h$ and $\widehat{\mathcal E}_h$ are equivalent to ${\mathcal F}$, but with $\gamma$ replaced by $\gamma Q(\mathbb{R}\backslash\{0\})$ in the definition of $Q_\theta$. Analogously, one can adjust the discrete-time experiments that we consider in Proposition \ref{prop2}. We leave the details to the reader.\vspace*{-2pt}
nodes.statement_short: If $Q$ has an atom at zero, Proposition 2.1 still holds with $\gamma$ replaced by $\gamma Q(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\})$.
nodes.label: whyQonoto

nodes.name: Discrete-time fully observed experiments ${\mathcal E}_{h,n,H_n}$
nodes.statement: To account for this phenomenon in discrete time, we introduce the following sequence of experiments, ${\mathcal E}_{h,n,H_n}$, indexed by $n\in\mathbb{N}$, where\vspace*{-2pt} \begin{equation} {\mathcal E}_{h,n,H_n} = \bigl([\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}]^2,{\mathcal B}([\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}]^2), ({\mathcal L}_{\theta} (G_n,h_n ) )_{\theta\in[0,\infty )^4} \bigr),\qquad n\in\mathbb{N} .\vspace*{-2pt} \end{equation} Here, $([0,\infty)^4,(H_n))$ is a parametrization of the full parameter space $[0,\infty)^4$; both $G_n=(G_{n,k})_{0\le k\le n}$ and $h_n=(h_{n,k})_{0\le k\le n}$ are defined by (\ref{G1}) via $H_n(\theta)=(h_{0,n}(\theta),\beta_n(\theta),\alpha_n(\theta ),\break\lambda_n(\theta))$ for $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\theta\in[0,\infty)^4$ (by a slight abuse of previous notation).

nodes.name: Fully observed GARCH experiments
nodes.statement: {\mathcal E}_{h,n,H_n} = \bigl([\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}]^2,{\mathcal B}([\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}]^2), ({\mathcal L}_{\theta} (G_n,h_n ) )_{\theta\in[0,\infty )^4} \bigr),\qquad n\in\mathbb{N} .\vspace*{-2pt}
nodes.label: experimentsh2

nodes.name: Proposition 2.2 (discrete-time analog)

nodes.name: Generic equivalence of GARCH and COGARCH with observed volatility
nodes.statement: Let us rephrase our results in terms of the GARCH experiments, with the volatility processes fully observed in both continuous and discrete time. In contrast to the situation in Theorem \ref{th1}, it follows from Proposition \ref{prop1} that the continuous-time experiments induced by (M)COGARCH are mutually equivalent in deficiency. Depending on the parametrization, (M)COGARCH also occurs as the limit in deficiency of discrete-time GARCH; in particular, this is the case for the parametrization in Proposition \ref{prop2}. In contrast to Theorem \ref{th1}, for a large class of parameter sets~$\Theta$, all of these discrete-time experiments, that is, ${\mathcal E}_{h,n,H^{(0)}_n}(\Theta)$, ${\mathcal E}_{h,n,H^{\mathrm{(KV)}}_n}(\Theta)$, ${\mathcal E}_{h,n,H_n^{\mathrm{(M)}}}(\Theta)$, are asymptotically equivalent to (M)COGARCH ${\mathcal E}_h(\Theta)$ and $\widehat{\mathcal E}_h(\Theta)$, in deficiency, as $n\to\infty$. This happens, for instance, if $\Theta\subseteq[0,\infty)^4$ does not contain an open neighborhood of $\Theta_{e}$. Since the set~$\Theta_e$ is of lower dimension than $[0,\infty)^4$ it is thus justified to say that the randomly thinned GARCH is \textit{generically} equivalent to COGARCH in deficiency as $n\to\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: With observed volatilities, randomly thinned GARCH is generically (off a lower-dimensional set) asymptotically equivalent to (M)COGARCH.

nodes.name: Extension to general Lévy drivers
nodes.statement: It would be interesting to extend the analysis to more general L\'{e}vy processes, rather than Brownian motion and compound Poisson processes. However, this would first require substantial investigations of the approximation and randomizations of L\'{e}vy processes themselves and, therefore, seems out of reach at the present stage of research.

nodes.name: Roadmap of the proof of Theorem 2.1

The proof is split into two parts, which appear in Sections \ref{proofth2} and \ref{SUBSECproofTh2PartII}, respectively. The second part uses a lemma which we formulate and prove in Section \ref{SUBSEC4.2}. To prove that ${\mathcal E}_{n,H_n^{(0)}} \to \hat{{\mathcal E}}$ in deficiency, we will introduce intermediate experiments ${\mathcal E}^{\star}_{1,n}$ and ${\mathcal E}^{\star}_{2,n}$. The first of\vspace*{1pt} these two experiments corresponds to a deterministic time grid, the latter to a randomized time grid. First, we will show that ${\mathcal E}_{n,H_n^{(0)}}$ is equivalent to ${\mathcal E}^{\star}_{1,n}$ in deficiency and then, using Lemma \ref{thinning} from Section~\ref{SUBSEC4.2}, that ${\mathcal E}^{\star}_{2,n}$ converges strongly to~$\widehat{\mathcal E}$. Finally, we will prove that ${\mathcal E}^{\star}_{1,n}$ and ${\mathcal E}^{\star}_{2,n}$ are equivalent.

nodes.statement: Suppose that (\ref{lre}) is satisfied for $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $p_n\in(0,1)$ and $\gamma\in(0,\infty)$. Let $B_{n,1}, \dots,B_{n,n}$ be independent Bernoulli variables with parameter $p_n$. Suppose that $(U_k,\zeta_{n,k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ is an i.i.d. sequence of random vectors with independent components, where~$U_k$ is uniformly distributed on $(0,1)$ and ${\mathcal L}(\zeta_{n,k})=Q_n$. Suppose that $B_{n,1}, \dots, B_{n,n}$ and $(U_k,\zeta_{n,k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ are independent. Observe that \[ {\mathcal L}(N_{2,n}) = {\mathcal L} \Biggl(\sum_{k=1}^n B_{n,k} \varepsilon _{(V_{n,k},\zeta_{n,k})} \Biggr) \] with $V_{n,k}=(k - 1+ U_k)/n$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and\vspace*{1pt} $1\le k\le n$. Let $\widehat N_n$ be a Poisson measure on $[0,1]\otimes\mathbb{R}$ with intensity measure $np_n\ell\otimes Q_n$ and define \[ \widehat N_{n,k}(B)=\widehat N_n \biggl(B\cap \biggl( \biggl(\frac{k - 1}n,\frac kn \biggr]\times\mathbb{R} \biggr) \biggr),\qquad B\in{\mathcal B} ([0,1]\times\mathbb{R}) . \] $\widehat N_{n,1},\dots,\widehat N_{n,n}$ are then independent Poisson point processes, where for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, \mbox{$1\le k\le n$}, $\widehat N_{n,k}$ has intensity measure \[ n p_n[\ell\otimes Q_n] \biggl(B\cap \biggl( \biggl(\frac{k - 1}n,\frac kn \biggr]\times\mathbb{R} \biggr) \biggr),\qquad B\in{\mathcal B}([0,1]\times\mathbb{R}) . \] By the monotonicity theorem for Markov kernels (see \cite{Re93}, Lemma 1.4.2(i)), observe that for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, \begin{equation} \|{\mathcal L}(N_{2,n})-{\mathcal L}(\widehat N_n)\| \le \Biggl\|\bigotimes_{k=1}^n{\mathcal L} \bigl(B_{n,k} \varepsilon_{(V_{n,k},\zeta_{n,k})} \bigr)-\bigotimes_{k=1}^n{\mathcal L} (\widehat N_{n,k} ) \Biggr\| . \end{equation} Denote the Hellinger distance between two probability measures $P_1$ and $P_2$ by $H(P_1,P_2)$. This gives us the following upper bound (see \cite{Re93}, Section~1.3, equation (1.23), and Section~1.3, equation (1.25)): \begin{eqnarray} &&\Biggl\|\bigotimes_{k=1}^n{\mathcal L} \bigl(B_{n,k} \varepsilon_{(V_{n,k},\zeta_{n,k})} \bigr)-\bigotimes_{k=1}^n{\mathcal L} (\widehat N_{n,k}) \Biggr\|\nonumber\\ &&\quad\le H \Biggl(\bigotimes_{k=1}^n{\mathcal L} \bigl(B_{n,k} \varepsilon_{(V_{n,k},\zeta_{n,k})} \bigr), \bigotimes_{k=1}^n{\mathcal L} (\widehat N_{n,k}) \Biggr)\\ &&\quad\le \Biggl(\sum_{k=1}^n H^2 \bigl({\mathcal L} \bigl(B_{n,k} \varepsilon_{(V_{n,k},\zeta_{n,k})} \bigr),{\mathcal L} (\widehat N_{n,k} ) \bigr) \Biggr)^{1/2}.\nonumber \end{eqnarray} Fix $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $1\le k\le n$. Let $(V_{n,k,l},\zeta_{n,k,l})_{l\in\mathbb{N}}$ be an i.i.d. sequence of random vectors with ${\mathcal L}(V_{n,k,l},\zeta_{n,k,l})={\mathcal L}(V_{n,k})\otimes Q_n$, $l\in\mathbb{N}$. Suppose that $(V_{n,k,l})$ is independent of $B_{n,k}$ and $\tau_{n,k}$, where $\tau_{n,k}$ is a Poisson\vadjust{\goodbreak} variable with parameter $p_n$. We then have the following identities: \[ {\mathcal L} \bigl(B_{n,k} \varepsilon_{(V_{n,k},\zeta_{n,k})} \bigr) = {\mathcal L} \Biggl(\sum_{l=1}^{B_{n,k}} \varepsilon_{(V_{n,k,l},\zeta_{n,k,l})} \Biggr),\qquad {\mathcal L} (\widehat N_{n,k}) = {\mathcal L} \Biggl(\sum_{l=1}^{\tau_{n,k}} \varepsilon_{(V_{n,k,l},\zeta_{n,k,l})} \Biggr) . \] By \cite{Re93}, Lemma 1.4.2(ii), for $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $1\le k\le n$, we must have \begin{equation} H \bigl({\mathcal L} \bigl(B_{n,k} \varepsilon_{(V_{n,k},Z_{n,k})} \bigr),{\mathcal L} (\widehat N_{n,k} ) \bigr) \le H({\mathcal L}(B_{n,k}),{\mathcal L}(\tau_{n,k})) . \end{equation} As $H({\mathcal L}(B_{n,k}),{\mathcal L}(\tau_{n,k}))\le3^{1/2}p_n$ (see \cite{Re93}, Theorem 1.3.1(ii)), it follows from (\ref{thin1})--(\ref{thin5}) and~(\ref{lre}) that \begin{equation} \limsup_{n\to\infty}\|{\mathcal L}(\tilde N_n)-{\mathcal L}(\hat N_n)\| \le \limsup_{n\to\infty}(3np_n^2)^{1/2}=0 . \end{equation} In view of a well-known upper bound of the laws of Poisson point measures in terms of the corresponding intensity measures (see \cite{Re93}, Section 3.2, equation (3.8)), it follows from (\ref{lre}) and $\|\ell\otimes Q\|=1$ that \begin{eqnarray*} \|{\mathcal L}(\widehat N_n)-{\mathcal L}(N)\| & \le& 3\|\gamma\ell\otimes Q-np_n\ell\otimes Q_n\|\\ & \le& 3 |np_n-\gamma| + 3 np_n \|Q-Q_n\| \to0\qquad \mbox{as } n\to\infty . \end{eqnarray*} By means of (\ref{thin6}) and (\ref{thin7}), this completes the proof of the lemma.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.2
nodes.statement:
By assumption, we have $f(x)=0$ for all $|x|\ge S$ and some $S>0$. Hence, there are $n_0=n_0(f,	heta)\in\mathbb{N}$ and $C_1=C_1(f,	heta)\in(1,\infty)$ such that for $C$ replaced by $C_1$, the assertion of Lemma ef{Lemexpectbound} holds. Let $n\ge n_0$, $i=1,2$, $	heta\in\Theta$, $1 \le k \le n$ and $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$. Recall (ef{defhatg}). In view of (ef{awayfromzero}), $\Psi_{i,n,	heta}\dvtx\mathbb{R}^k	o\mathbb{R}^k$ is a\vadjust{\goodbreak} well defined $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism, where $\Psi_{i,n,\sigma,	heta}=(\psi_{i,n,l,\sigma,	heta})_{1\le l\le k}\dvtx reak\mathbb{R}^k	o\mathbb{R}^k$ is defined by  egin{eqnarray} \psi_{i,n,l,\sigma,	heta}(y)= rac{y_l}{\hat g^{1/2}_{i,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)} \end{eqnarray} for $y=(y_1,\dots,y_k)\in\mathbb{R}^k$ and $1\le l\le k$. For all $n\ge n_0$, $	heta\in\Theta$, $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$ and $\sigma \in M_{n,k}$, we define \[ 	ilde f_{i,n,k,\sigma,	heta}(y) = \prod_{l=1}^k  rac{f(\psi_{i,n,l,\sigma,	heta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{i,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)},\qquad y\in\mathbb{R}^k , i=1,2 . \] It follows from (ef{defhatg}), (ef{Yip}) and (ef{Phiip}) that $	ilde f_{i,n,k,\sigma,	heta}$ is a density of the probability measure ${\mathcal L}_	heta (Y_{i,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} )$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure $\ell^{\otimes k}$ on ${\mathcal B}(\mathbb{R}^k)$. In particular, we must have  egin{equation}  igl\|{\mathcal L}_	heta (Y_{1,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} ) -{\mathcal L}_	heta (Y_{2,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} )  igr\| =  rac 12\int_{\mathbb{R}^k}|	ilde f_{1,n,k,\sigma,	heta}(y)-	ilde f_{2,n,k,\sigma,	heta}(y)|\,\mathrm{d}y \end{equation} for all $	heta\in\Theta$, $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$ and $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$. Suppose that $C_f\in(0,\infty)$ is a global Lipschitz constant of $f$. By means of simple substitutions, for all $\epsilon>0$ and $w, v\ge\epsilon$, we can observe that \[  rac 12 \int  iggl| rac{f(x/v)}{v}- rac{f(x/w)}{w}  iggr|\,\mathrm{d}x \le  rac1 \epsilon (S^2 C_f+1) |v-w| . \] Consequently, for all $\epsilon>0$, we find a $\kappa_1=\kappa_1(f,\epsilon)\in(1,\infty)$ such that \[  rac12 \int  iggl| rac{f(x/v)}{v}- rac{f(x/w)}{w}  iggr|\,\mathrm{d}x \le \kappa_1(\epsilon)|v-w|,\qquad v,w\ge\epsilon . \] In view of (ef{awayfromzero}), there thus exists some $\kappa_2=\kappa_2(f,\Theta)\in(1,\infty)$ such that  egin{eqnarray} && rac12 \int  iggl| rac{f(y_l/\hat g^{1/2}_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y))}{\hat g_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}^{1/2}(y)}-  rac{f(y_l/\hat g^{1/2}_{2,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{2,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)}  iggr|\,\mathrm{d}y_l
onumber\ [-8pt]\ [-8pt] &&\quad\le\kappa_2|\hat g_{1,n,{l - 1},\sigma,	heta}(y)-\hat g_{2,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)|
onumber \end{eqnarray} for all $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$, $1 \le l\le k$, $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$, $y\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ and $	heta\in\Theta$. By integrating over $y_k$, we get from (ef{cinproof}) that  egin{eqnarray} && rac12\int_{\mathbb{R}^k}|	ilde f_{1,n,k,\sigma,	heta}(y)-	ilde f_{2,n,k,\sigma,	heta}(y)|\,\mathrm{d}y
onumber\ &&\quad\le \kappa_2\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k - 1}}\prod_{l=1}^{k-1}  rac{f(\psi_{1,n,l,\sigma,	heta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)} |\hat g_{1,n,k - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)- \hat g_{2,n,k - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y) |\,\mathrm{d}y\ &&\qquad{} + rac12\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k - 1}} \Biggl|\prod_{l=1}^{k-1}  rac{f(\psi_{1,n,l,\sigma,	heta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)}- \prod_{l=1}^{k-1}  rac{f(\psi_{2,n,l,\sigma,	heta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{2,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)} \Biggr|\,\mathrm{d}y
onumber \end{eqnarray} for all $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$, $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$ and $	heta\in\Theta$. It follows from (ef{hatcondEgdiff}) that  egin{eqnarray} && \int_{\mathbb{R}^{k - 1}}\prod_{l=1}^{k-1}  rac{f(\psi_{1,n,l,\sigma,	heta}(y))}{g^{1/2}_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma ,	heta}(y)} |\hat g_{1,n,k - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)- \hat g_{2,n,k - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y) |\,\mathrm{d}y
onumber\ [-8pt]\ [-8pt] &&\quad=E_	heta [ |\hat g_{1,n,k - 1,	heta}(Y_{1,n})- \hat g_{2,n,k - 1,	heta}(Y_{1,n}) | |A_{n,k,\sigma}]\le  rac{C_1^k}n
onumber \end{eqnarray} for all $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$, $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$ and $	heta\in\Theta$. Let $C=\mathrm{e} \kappa_2 C_1$. By induction, we thus get from (ef{hatg0diff}) and (ef{cinproof2})--(ef{cinproof3}) that \[  igl \|{\mathcal L}_	heta (Y_{1,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} )-{\mathcal L} _	heta (Y_{2,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} )  igr\| \le rac{C^k}{n} , \] uniformly for all $n\,{\ge}\,n_0, 1\,{\le}\,k\,{\le}\,n, \sigma\,{\in}\,M_{n,k}$ and $	heta\,{\in}\,\Theta$. This completes the proof of the~lemma.\vspace*{-3pt}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.2 (part II)
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a Lebesgue density of $Q$ and $\Theta$ be as in Theorem \ref{th2a}. We denote the positive part of a function $g\dvtx\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ by $g^+$. Let $C^\infty_C$ be the space of infinitely often continuously differentiable functions $g\dvtx\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ with compact support $\overline{\{g>0\}}$. As $C^\infty_C$ is dense in $L^1$, we find a sequence of $g_m\in C_C^\infty$, $m\in\mathbb{N}$, such that $\int|g_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell\to0$ as $m\to\infty$. It is immediate that both $\int|g_m^+-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell\to0$ and $\int g_m^+\,\mathrm{d}\ell\to1$ as $m\to \infty$. Without loss of generality, we may thus assume that $\int g_m^+\,\mathrm{d}\ell>0$ for all $m\in\mathbb{N}$. Then, $h_m:=g^+_m/\int g_m^+\,\mathrm{d}\ell$ defines a sequence of globally Lipschitz continuous probability densities with a compact support $\overline{\{h_m>0\}}$ such that $\int|h_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell\to0$. For $m\in\mathbb{N}$, let $Z^{(m)}_n=(Z^{(m)}_{n,k})_{1\le k\le n}$ be a random vector with distribution \[ {\mathcal L}\bigl(Z^{(m)}_n\bigr)(B) = \biggl((1 - p_n)\varepsilon_0(B)+p_n \int _Bh_m\,\mathrm{d}\ell \biggr)^{\otimes n} , \] with $B\in{\mathcal B}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, $1\le k\le n$. If we replace $Z_{n,k}$ by $Z^{(m)}_{n,k}$ in (\ref{Xip}), then we get yet another family of GARCH models, $X^{(m)}_{i,n}=(X^{(m)}_{i,n}(k))_{1\le k\le n}$, say, indexed by $\theta\in\Theta$, $i=1,2$ and $m$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$. It follows from the monotonicity theorem for Markov kernels and a well-known upper bound for product measures (see \cite{Re93}, Lemma 1.4.2(i) and page 23) that for all \mbox{$i=1,2$}, \begin{eqnarray} \hspace*{-15pt}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\bigl\|{\mathcal L}_\theta(X_{i,n})-{\mathcal L} _\theta\bigl(X^{(m)}_{i,n}\bigr)\bigr\| &\le& \bigl\|{\mathcal L}(Z_{n})-{\mathcal L}\bigl(Z^{(m)}_n\bigr)\bigr\|\nonumber\\ [-8pt]\\ [-8pt] \hspace*{-15pt}&\le& n\bigl\|{\mathcal L}(Z_{n,1})-{\mathcal L}\bigl(Z^{(m)}_{n,1}\bigr)\bigr\|= \frac{n p_n}2 \int|h_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell .\nonumber \end{eqnarray}\looseness=0 As $h_m$ is globally Lipschitz with a compact support $\overline{\{h_m>0\}}$ for all $m\in\mathbb{N}_0$, the assumptions of Lemma \ref{condTVlem} hold. For all $m\in\mathbb{N}$, there thus exist $n_m\in\mathbb{N}$ and $C_m=C(h_m,\Theta)\in(0,\infty)$ such that for all $n\ge n_m$, we get, by conditioning and the monotonicity theorem for Markov kernels, that \begin{equation} \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\bigl\|{\mathcal L}_\theta \bigl(X^{(m)}_{1,n}\bigr)-{\mathcal L}_\theta\bigl(X^{(m)}_{2,n}\bigr)\bigr\| \le \frac 1n E \bigl[C_m^{\|N_n\|} \bigr] \end{equation} for $N_n$ as defined in (\ref{defNn}). Recall (\ref{Xip}). By combining (\ref{truncatednoise}) and (\ref{condTV1}), we get, from the triangle inequality, that \[ \sup_{\theta\in\Theta} \bigl\|{\mathcal L}_\theta(G_n)-{\mathcal L}_\theta \bigl(G_n^{(0)}\bigr) \bigr\| \le n p_n \int|h_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell+\frac1n E \bigl[C_m^{\|N_n\|} \bigr] \] for all $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and $n\ge n_m$. As (\ref{lre}) holds, we have $\lim_{n\to\infty}EC_m^{\|N_n\|}= e^{\lambda(C_m-1)}$ and thus \[ \limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta} \bigl\|{\mathcal L}_\theta (G_n)-{\mathcal L}_\theta\bigl(G_n^{(0)}\bigr) \bigr\| \le\lambda \limsup_{m\to\infty}\int|h_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell=0 , \] giving (\ref{th2astronger}). This completes the proof of Theorem \ref{th2a} in the case where $Q_n=Q$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ (see (\ref{QnequalsQ})). Now, assume that $Q_n\to Q$ in total variation norm as $n\to\infty$. For $m\in\mathbb{N}$, let $\widehat Z_n=(\widehat Z_{n,k})_{1\le k\le n}$ be a random vector with distribution \[ {\mathcal L}(\widehat Z_n) = \bigl((1 - p_n)\varepsilon_0+p_n Q_n \bigr)^{\otimes n},\qquad n\in\mathbb{N} . \] If we replace $Z_{n,k}$ by $\widehat Z_{n,k}$ in (\ref{Xip}), then we get the GARCH models in the assertion of the theorem. We denote them by $\widehat X_{i,n}$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $i=1,2$. By the same argument as in~(\ref{truncatednoise}), we must have, for all $i=1,2$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , \[ \sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\|{\mathcal L}_\theta(\widehat {X}_{i,n})-{\mathcal L}_\theta(X_{i,n})\| \le np_n\|Q_n-Q\| . \] As the right-hand side tends to zero, this completes the proof of the theorem.

nodes.statement:
For $f\in D_d[0,1]$, we write $\Delta f=f(t)-f(t-)$, $0\le t\le1$, with the convention that $\Delta f(0)=0$. With the usual convention $\inf\varnothing=\infty$, we define $T(f)=\inf\{t\in[0,1]\dvtx\Delta f_1(t)
eq0\}\wedge1$ for all $f=(f_1,f_2)\in D_2$. Let $S$ be the set of all functions $f\in D_2$ with $T(f)\in(0,1)$. Let $D''_{0}\subseteq D_2[0,1]$ be the set of all functions $f=(f_1,f_2)$ such that the right-hand derivatives~$f'_1(0+)$ and $f''_2(0+)$ exist in $\mathbb{R}$. Further, let $D''_{0,T}\subseteq S\cap D_0''$ be the set of all functions $f=(f_1,f_2)$ such that the right-hand derivatives $f'_2(T(f)+)$ and $f''_2(T(f)+)$ exist in $\mathbb{R}$. Let $f\in D_2$ with $T=T(f)$. If $f\in D''_{0,T}$ and $f'_2(0+)
eq0$, then we set \[ X(f) =  iggl(|f_2(0)|,  iggl| rac{(f_2'(0+))^2 - f_2(0)f_2''(0+)}{f'_2(0+)}  iggr|,  iggl| rac{f_2''(0+)}{f'_2(0+)}  iggr|, rac{|\Delta f_2(T)|}{(\Delta f_1(T))^2}  iggr) . \] If $f\in D''_{0,T}$, $f'_2(0+)= 0$ and $f'_2(T+)
eq0$, then we set \[ X(f) =  iggl(|f_2(0)|,  iggl| rac{(f_2'(T+))^2 - f_2(T)f_2''(T+)}{f'_2(T+)}  iggr|,  iggl| rac{f_2''(T+)}{f'_2(T+)}  iggr|, rac{|\Delta f_2(T)|}{(\Delta f_1(T))^2}  iggr) . \] If $f\in D''_{0,T}$, $f'(0+)=f'_2(T+)=0$ and $\Delta f_2(T)
eq0$, then we set \[ X(f) =  iggl(|f_2(0)|,0,0 , rac{|\Delta f_2(T)|}{(\Delta f_1(T))^2}  iggr) .\vadjust{\goodbreak} \] If $f\in D''_{0,T}$, $f'(0+)=f'_2(T+)=0$ and $\Delta f_2(T)= 0$, then we set $X(f)=(|f_2(0)|,\infty,\infty,0)$. If $f\in D''_{0} ackslash S$ and $f'_2(0+)
eq0$, then we define \[ X(f) =  iggl(|f_2(0)|,  iggl| rac{(f_2'(0+))^2 - f_2(0)f_2''(0+)}{f'_2(0+)}  iggr|,  iggl| rac{f_2''(0+)}{f'_2(0+)}  iggr|,\infty  iggr) . \] For the remaining cases, we set $X(f)= (|f_2(0)|,\infty,\infty,\infty )$. Then, $X\dvtx D_2	o[0,\infty]^4$ is a ${\mathcal D}_2$-${\mathcal B}([0,\infty]^4)$-measurable mapping. Since $Q(\{0\})=0$, it follows from (ef{COG}) that ${\mathcal L}_	heta^X((G,h))=Q_{	heta}$ for all $	heta\in[0,\infty)^4$ and thus $\delta({\mathcal E}_{h},{\mathcal F})=0$ by (ef{defMarkov}), where ${\mathcal F}$ is the experiment as defined in the assertion of the proposition. Next, we show that $\delta({\mathcal F},{\mathcal E}_h)=0$. To this end, we define $\xi=(\xi_1,\dots,\xi_3)\dvtx[0,\infty]^4	o[0,\infty)^3$ as follows. nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.3
nodes.statement: (i) Define $X,X_n\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\to[0,\infty]^4$ as follows. If $\omega=(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_4)\in[0,\infty)^3\times\{\infty\} $ such that $\omega_1\omega_3=\omega_2$, then set $X(\omega)=(\omega_1,\infty,\infty,\infty)$; otherwise, set $X(\omega)=\omega$. If $\omega=(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_4)\in [0,\infty)^3\times\{\infty\}$ such that $\omega_1 n(1-\mathrm{e}^{-\omega_3/n})=\omega_2$, then set $X_n(\omega)=(\omega_1,\infty,\infty,\infty)$; otherwise, set $X_n(\omega)=\omega$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$. By definition, the deficiency is non-decreasing in the parameter set with respect to set inclusions. Further, we have $\widehat Q^X_{\theta}=Q_{\theta}$ and $\widehat Q^{X_n}_{\theta}= Q_{\theta,n}$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and thus, by~(\ref{defMarkov}), $\delta(\widehat{\mathcal F}(\Theta),{\mathcal F}(\Theta))\le \delta(\widehat{\mathcal F},{\mathcal F})=0$ and $\delta(\widehat{\mathcal F}(\Theta),{\mathcal F}_n(\Theta))\le \delta(\widehat{\mathcal F},{\mathcal F}_n)=0$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, completing the proof of (i). (ii) First, assume that $\Theta$ satisfies (\ref{hsgleichbetaalphagleich}) for all $x>0$. Without loss of generality, we may assume that $\Theta\subseteq[0,\infty)^4$ is a finite set (see \cite{St85}, Theorem 51.4). Define $\Omega_\Theta$ to be the set of all $\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4) \in(0,\infty)\times\{\infty\}^2\times\{0,\infty\}$ such that $( \omega_1,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in(\Theta\cap\Theta_e)\backslash \widehat\Theta_e$ for some $(\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in[0,\infty)^3$. If $\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4)\in\Omega_\Theta$, then it follows from (\ref{hsgleichbetaalphagleich}) that the corresponding pair $(\beta,\alpha)=(\beta(\omega_1),\alpha(\omega_1))\in [0,\infty)^2$ is uniquely determined by $\omega_1$. Hence, we may define a mapping $Y\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\to[0,\infty]^4$ as follows: if $\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4)\in\Omega_\Theta$, then we set $Y(\omega)=( \omega_1,\beta(\omega_1),\alpha(\omega_1),\omega_4)$; otherwise, if $\omega\in[0,\infty]^4\backslash\Omega_\Theta$, then we set $Y(\omega)=\omega$. As $\Theta$, and thus $\Omega_\Theta$, is a finite set, the mapping $Y$ is ${\mathcal B}([0,\infty]^4)/{\mathcal B}([0,\infty]^4)$-measurable. In view of (\ref{hsgleichbetaalphagleich}), note that $Q^Y_\theta=\widehat Q_\theta$ for all $\theta\in\Theta$ and thus $\delta({\mathcal F}(\Theta),\widehat{\mathcal F}(\Theta))=0$, by~(\ref{defMarkov}). Second, assume that (\ref{hsgleichbetaalphagleich}) is violated. There then exist some $h_0 > 0$, $\theta_1=(h_{0},\beta_1,\alpha_2,\lambda_1)$ $\in\Theta\cap\Theta_{e}\cap\widehat\Theta_{e}^C$ and $\theta_2=(h_{0},\beta_2,\alpha_2,\lambda_2)\in\Theta\cap\Theta_{e}$ such that $(\beta_1,\alpha_{1})\neq(\beta_2,\alpha_{2})$. Consider $\Theta_{0}=\{\theta_{1},\theta_{2}\}$ and the decision space $D=\{(\beta_1,\alpha_1),(\beta_2,\alpha_2)\}$, endowed with the discrete topology. For $\theta=(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in\Theta$, consider (continuous and bounded) loss functions $W_\theta\dvtx D\to\mathbb{R}$, where for $x=(x_1,\dots,x_4)\in[0,\infty]^4$, we set $W_{\theta}(x)=1-1_{\{(\beta,\alpha)\}}(x_2,x_3)$. Further, we define a Markov kernel $\widehat\rho\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\times{\mathcal B}(D)\to[0,1]$, where for $x\in[0,\infty]^4$ and $B\in{\mathcal B}(D)$, we set \[ \widehat\rho(x,B) = \cases{ \epsilon_{(\beta_1,\alpha_1)}(B) ,&\quad if $x\in(0,\infty)\times \{\beta_1\}\times\{\alpha_1\}\times[0,\infty)$,\cr \epsilon_{(\beta_2,\alpha_2)}(B) ,&\quad otherwise. } \] We then have $\int W_{\theta_i}(x) \widehat\rho(\omega,\mathrm{d}x) \widehat Q_{\theta_i}(\mathrm{d}\omega)=0$ for $i = 1,2$. On the other hand, any Markov kernel $\rho\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\times{\mathcal B}(D)\to[0,1]$ is of the form $\rho(\omega,B)=p(\omega)\epsilon_{(\beta_1,\alpha_1)}(B)+ (1-p(\omega))\epsilon_{(\beta_2,\alpha_2)}(B)$, where $p\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\to[0,1]$ is Borel, $\omega\in[0,\infty]^4$ and $B\in{\mathcal B}(D)$. It is easy to see that for such a Markov kernel $\rho$, there exists a Markov kernel $ \bar\rho\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\times {\mathcal B}(D)\to[0,1]$ such that both \[ \int W_{\theta_1}(x) \rho(\omega,\mathrm{d}x) Q_{\theta_1}(\mathrm{d}\omega)\ge \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma} \bigl(1-p(h_0,\infty,\infty,\infty)\bigr) \] and \[ \hspace*{-22pt}\int W_{\theta_2}(x) \rho(\omega,\mathrm{d}x) Q_{\theta_2}(\mathrm{d}\omega)\ge \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}p(h_0,\infty,\infty,\infty) . \] In view of (\ref{defdeffic}), we thus have $\delta({\mathcal F}(\Theta),\widehat{\mathcal F}(\Theta))\ge \delta({\mathcal F}(\Theta_0),{\mathcal F}(\Theta_0))\ge \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}/2$, which completes the proof of (ii). (iii) This follows by the same arguments as in (ii).
