nodes.name: Statistical experiment
nodes.statement: Let $\Theta$ be a non-empty set, $(E,{\mathcal A})$ be a measurable space and $(P_{\theta})_{\theta\in\Theta}$ be a family of probability measures on ${\mathcal A}$. The triplet ${\mathcal E}=(E,{\mathcal A},(P_{\theta})_{\theta\in\Theta})$ is then called a~(statistical) experiment. Consider two experiments ${\mathcal E}_i=(E_i,{\mathcal A}_i,(P_{i,\theta})_{\theta\in\Theta})$, $i=1,2$, indexed by $\Theta$.

nodes.name: Decision problem
nodes.statement: A decision problem is a triple $(\Theta,D,W)$, where $D$ is a topological space and $W=(W_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ is a loss function $W_\theta\dvtx D\to\mathbb{R}$, $\theta\in\Theta$.

nodes.name: $\epsilon$-deficiency
nodes.statement: Let $\|W_\theta\|_{\infty}=\sup_{d\in D}|W_\theta(d)|$. Also, let $\epsilon\ge0$. Then, ${\mathcal E}_1$ is called $\epsilon$-\textit{deficient with respect to} ${\mathcal E}_2$, notated as ${\mathcal E}_1\supseteq_\epsilon {\mathcal E}_2$, if and only if for all decision problems $(\Theta,D,W)$ with $W$ continuous and bounded, and all $\beta_2\in{\mathcal B}({\mathcal E}_2,D)$, there exists some $\beta_1\in{\mathcal B}({\mathcal E}_1,D)$ such that\looseness=-1 \[ \beta_1(W_\theta,P_{1,\theta})\le\beta_2(W_\theta,P_{2,\theta })+\epsilon\|W_\theta\|_{\infty} ,\qquad \theta\in\Theta , \]\looseness=0 where ${\mathcal B}({\mathcal E}_i,D)$ ($i=1,2$) is the space of generalized decision functions (see \cite{St85}, Definition~42.2).
nodes.statement_short: ${\mathcal E}_1$ is $\epsilon$-deficient w.r.t. ${\mathcal E}_2$ if every decision rule of ${\mathcal E}_2$ is matched by one of ${\mathcal E}_1$ up to risk $\epsilon\|W\|_\infty$.

nodes.name: Deficiency $\delta$
nodes.statement: The deficiency of ${\mathcal E}_1$ with respect to ${\mathcal E}_2$ is the number \begin{equation} \delta({\mathcal E}_1,{\mathcal E}_2) = \inf\{\epsilon>0 \dvtx {\mathcal E}_1\supseteq _\epsilon {\mathcal E}_2\} . \end{equation}

nodes.name: Deficiency
nodes.statement: \delta({\mathcal E}_1,{\mathcal E}_2) = \inf\{\epsilon>0 \dvtx {\mathcal E}_1\supseteq _\epsilon {\mathcal E}_2\} .
nodes.label: defdeffic

nodes.name: Equivalence in deficiency
nodes.statement: Two experiments ${\mathcal E}_1$ and ${\mathcal E}_2$ are called \textit{equivalent in deficiency} if and only if ${\mathcal E}_1\supseteq_0 {\mathcal E}_2$ and ${\mathcal E}_2\supseteq_0 {\mathcal E}_1$.

nodes.name: Markov-kernel representation of deficiency (Strasser, Lemma 55.4)
nodes.statement: \delta({\mathcal E}_1,{\mathcal E}_2) = \inf_K \sup_{\theta\in\Theta} \| P_{2,\theta} - K P_{1,\theta} \|
nodes.statement_short: Deficiency equals the best uniform TV approximation of ${\mathcal E}_2$ by Markov-kernel images of ${\mathcal E}_1$.
nodes.label: defMarkov

nodes.name: Le Cam's distance
nodes.statement: Le Cam's distance between ${\mathcal E}_1$ and ${\mathcal E}_2$ is a pseudo-metric on the space of all experiments indexed by $\Theta$ (see \cite{St85}, Corollary 59.6), defined by setting \begin{equation} \Delta({\mathcal E}_1,{\mathcal E}_2) = \max\{ \delta({\mathcal E}_1,{\mathcal E}_2),\delta({\mathcal E}_2,{\mathcal E}_1) \}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Le Cam's distance
nodes.statement: \Delta({\mathcal E}_1,{\mathcal E}_2) = \max\{ \delta({\mathcal E}_1,{\mathcal E}_2),\delta({\mathcal E}_2,{\mathcal E}_1) \}.
nodes.label: deflecam

nodes.name: Le Cam distance bounded by total variation (Strasser, Corollary 59.6)
nodes.statement: \Delta({\mathcal E}_1,{\mathcal E}_2) \le \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|P_{1,\theta}-P_{2,\theta}\| .
assumptions: If $(E_1,{\mathcal A}_1)=(E_2,{\mathcal A}_2)$
nodes.label: deflecamsmallerTV

nodes.name: Equivalence iff zero Le Cam distance
nodes.statement: Clearly, if ${\mathcal E}_1$ and ${\mathcal E}_2$ are two experiments indexed by the same $\Theta$, then ${\mathcal E}_1$ is equivalent to ${\mathcal E}_2$ in deficiency if and only if $\Delta({\mathcal E}_1,{\mathcal E}_2)=0$.
assumptions: ${\mathcal E}_1$ and ${\mathcal E}_2$ are two experiments indexed by the same $\Theta$
conclusions: ${\mathcal E}_1$ is equivalent to ${\mathcal E}_2$ in deficiency if and only if $\Delta({\mathcal E}_1,{\mathcal E}_2)=0$

nodes.name: Strong convergence and asymptotic equivalence in deficiency
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathcal E}$, ${\mathcal E}_n$, ${\mathcal F}_n$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$, be experiments, all indexed by $\Theta$. We then say that ${\mathcal E}_n$ converges (strongly) in deficiency, or that ${\mathcal E}_n$ and~${\mathcal F}_n$ are (strongly) asymptotically equivalent in deficiency, if and only if $\Delta({\mathcal E}_n,{\mathcal E}) \to0$ and $\Delta({\mathcal E}_n,{\mathcal F}_n) \to0$, respectively, as $n\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Subexperiments ${\mathcal E}(\Theta_0)$
nodes.statement: For $\varnothing\neq\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, we employ the notation ${\mathcal E}(\Theta_0)=(E,{\mathcal A},(P_{\theta})_{\theta_\in\Theta_0})$ for corresponding subexperiments of ${\mathcal E}=(E,{\mathcal A},(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$.

nodes.name: Weak convergence in deficiency
nodes.statement: We refer to weak convergence and weak asymptotic equivalence in deficiency if and only if, for all non-empty and finite $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the corresponding subexperiments converge strongly and are strongly asymptotically equivalent in deficiency, respectively.

nodes.name: Represent $N_{2,n}$ via Bernoulli thinning variables
nodes.statement: Suppose that (\ref{lre}) is satisfied for $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $p_n\in(0,1)$ and $\gamma\in(0,\infty)$. Let $B_{n,1}, \dots,B_{n,n}$ be independent Bernoulli variables with parameter $p_n$. Suppose that $(U_k,\zeta_{n,k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ is an i.i.d. sequence of random vectors with independent components, where~$U_k$ is uniformly distributed on $(0,1)$ and ${\mathcal L}(\zeta_{n,k})=Q_n$. Suppose that $B_{n,1}, \dots, B_{n,n}$ and $(U_k,\zeta_{n,k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ are independent. Observe that \[ {\mathcal L}(N_{2,n}) = {\mathcal L} \Biggl(\sum_{k=1}^n B_{n,k} \varepsilon _{(V_{n,k},\zeta_{n,k})} \Biggr) \] with $V_{n,k}=(k - 1+ U_k)/n$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and\vspace*{1pt} $1\le k\le n$.
nodes.statement_short: Represent $N_{2,n}$ via Bernoulli thinning variables

nodes.name: Introduce Poisson process $\widehat N_n$ split into independ
nodes.statement: Let $\widehat N_n$ be a Poisson measure on $[0,1]\otimes\mathbb{R}$ with intensity measure $np_n\ell\otimes Q_n$ and define \[ \widehat N_{n,k}(B)=\widehat N_n \biggl(B\cap \biggl( \biggl(\frac{k - 1}n,\frac kn \biggr]\times\mathbb{R} \biggr) \biggr),\qquad B\in{\mathcal B} ([0,1]\times\mathbb{R}) . \] $\widehat N_{n,1},\dots,\widehat N_{n,n}$ are then independent Poisson point processes, where for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, \mbox{$1\le k\le n$}, $\widehat N_{n,k}$ has intensity measure \[ n p_n[\ell\otimes Q_n] \biggl(B\cap \biggl( \biggl(\frac{k - 1}n,\frac kn \biggr]\times\mathbb{R} \biggr) \biggr),\qquad B\in{\mathcal B}([0,1]\times\mathbb{R}) . \]
nodes.statement_short: Introduce Poisson process $\widehat N_n$ split into independent cells

nodes.name: Bound TV by product of cell laws (monotonicity theorem)
nodes.statement: By the monotonicity theorem for Markov kernels (see \cite{Re93}, Lemma 1.4.2(i)), observe that for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, \begin{equation} \|{\mathcal L}(N_{2,n})-{\mathcal L}(\widehat N_n)\| \le \Biggl\|\bigotimes_{k=1}^n{\mathcal L} \bigl(B_{n,k} \varepsilon_{(V_{n,k},\zeta_{n,k})} \bigr)-\bigotimes_{k=1}^n{\mathcal L} (\widehat N_{n,k} ) \Biggr\| . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Bound TV by product of cell laws (monotonicity theorem)

nodes.name: Bound TV by Hellinger distance of products
nodes.statement: Denote the Hellinger distance between two probability measures $P_1$ and $P_2$ by $H(P_1,P_2)$. This gives us the following upper bound (see \cite{Re93}, Section~1.3, equation (1.23), and Section~1.3, equation (1.25)): \begin{eqnarray} &&\Biggl\|\bigotimes_{k=1}^n{\mathcal L} \bigl(B_{n,k} \varepsilon_{(V_{n,k},\zeta_{n,k})} \bigr)-\bigotimes_{k=1}^n{\mathcal L} (\widehat N_{n,k}) \Biggr\|\nonumber\\ &&\quad\le H \Biggl(\bigotimes_{k=1}^n{\mathcal L} \bigl(B_{n,k} \varepsilon_{(V_{n,k},\zeta_{n,k})} \bigr), \bigotimes_{k=1}^n{\mathcal L} (\widehat N_{n,k}) \Biggr)\\ &&\quad\le \Biggl(\sum_{k=1}^n H^2 \bigl({\mathcal L} \bigl(B_{n,k} \varepsilon_{(V_{n,k},\zeta_{n,k})} \bigr),{\mathcal L} (\widehat N_{n,k} ) \bigr) \Biggr)^{1/2}.\nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Bound TV by Hellinger distance of products

nodes.name: Represent cell laws as Bernoulli vs. Poisson random sums
nodes.statement: Fix $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $1\le k\le n$. Let $(V_{n,k,l},\zeta_{n,k,l})_{l\in\mathbb{N}}$ be an i.i.d. sequence of random vectors with ${\mathcal L}(V_{n,k,l},\zeta_{n,k,l})={\mathcal L}(V_{n,k})\otimes Q_n$, $l\in\mathbb{N}$. Suppose that $(V_{n,k,l})$ is independent of $B_{n,k}$ and $\tau_{n,k}$, where $\tau_{n,k}$ is a Poisson\vadjust{\goodbreak} variable with parameter $p_n$. We then have the following identities: \[ {\mathcal L} \bigl(B_{n,k} \varepsilon_{(V_{n,k},\zeta_{n,k})} \bigr) = {\mathcal L} \Biggl(\sum_{l=1}^{B_{n,k}} \varepsilon_{(V_{n,k,l},\zeta_{n,k,l})} \Biggr),\qquad {\mathcal L} (\widehat N_{n,k}) = {\mathcal L} \Biggl(\sum_{l=1}^{\tau_{n,k}} \varepsilon_{(V_{n,k,l},\zeta_{n,k,l})} \Biggr) . \]
nodes.statement_short: Represent cell laws as Bernoulli vs. Poisson random sums

nodes.name: Reduce to Hellinger distance of counts
nodes.statement: By \cite{Re93}, Lemma 1.4.2(ii), for $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $1\le k\le n$, we must have \begin{equation} H \bigl({\mathcal L} \bigl(B_{n,k} \varepsilon_{(V_{n,k},Z_{n,k})} \bigr),{\mathcal L} (\widehat N_{n,k} ) \bigr) \le H({\mathcal L}(B_{n,k}),{\mathcal L}(\tau_{n,k})) . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Hellinger distance of counts

nodes.name: Show $N_{2,n}$ and $\widehat N_n$ merge as $np_n^2\to0$
nodes.statement: As $H({\mathcal L}(B_{n,k}),{\mathcal L}(\tau_{n,k}))\le3^{1/2}p_n$ (see \cite{Re93}, Theorem 1.3.1(ii)), it follows from (\ref{thin1})--(\ref{thin5}) and~(\ref{lre}) that \begin{equation} \limsup_{n\to\infty}\|{\mathcal L}(\tilde N_n)-{\mathcal L}(\hat N_n)\| \le \limsup_{n\to\infty}(3np_n^2)^{1/2}=0 . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Show $N_{2,n}$ and $\widehat N_n$ merge as $np_n^2\to0$

nodes.name: Bound $\widehat N_n$ vs. $N$ by intensities and conclude
nodes.statement: In view of a well-known upper bound of the laws of Poisson point measures in terms of the corresponding intensity measures (see \cite{Re93}, Section 3.2, equation (3.8)), it follows from (\ref{lre}) and $\|\ell\otimes Q\|=1$ that \begin{eqnarray*} \|{\mathcal L}(\widehat N_n)-{\mathcal L}(N)\| & \le& 3\|\gamma\ell\otimes Q-np_n\ell\otimes Q_n\|\\ & \le& 3 |np_n-\gamma| + 3 np_n \|Q-Q_n\| \to0\qquad \mbox{as } n\to\infty . \end{eqnarray*} By means of (\ref{thin6}) and (\ref{thin7}), this completes the proof of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\widehat N_n$ vs. $N$ by intensities and conclude

nodes.name: Define point measure $N_{1,n}$ of thinned innovations
nodes.statement: For $n\in\mathbb{N}$, define a point measure $N_{1,n}$ on $[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}$ by \begin{equation} N_{1,n}=\sum_{k=1}^n 1_{Z_{n,k}\neq 0} \varepsilon_{(k/n , Z_{n,k})},\qquad n\in\mathbb{N} . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Define point measure $N_{1,n}$ of thinned innovations

nodes.name: Define continuous-time experiment ${\mathcal E}^\star_{1,n}$
nodes.statement: Using $N_{1,n}$, we pass from discrete to continuous time. For $n\in\mathbb{N}$, define \[ {\mathcal E}^{\star}_{1,n}=\bigl(D_1,{\mathcal D}_1,({\mathcal L}_\theta(G_{1,n}))_{\theta \in[0,\infty)^4}\bigr), \] where, for all $0\le t\le1$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\theta=(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in[0,\infty)^4$, $(G_{1,n},h_{1,n})$ is the unique pathwise solution of the following system of integral equations ($t\in[0,1]$): \begin{eqnarray} G_{1,n}(t) & = & \int_{[0,t]\times\mathbb{R}} h^{1/2}_{1,n}(s-) z N_{1,n}(\mathrm{d}s,\mathrm{d}z) ,\nonumber\\ [-10pt]\\ [-10pt] h_{1,n}(t) & = & h_0 + \int_{[0,t]} \beta- \alpha h_{1,n}(s-)\,\mathrm{d}s + \lambda\int_{[0,t]\times\mathbb{R}} h_{1,n}(s-)z^2 N_{1,n}(\mathrm{d}s,\mathrm{d}z).\nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Define continuous-time experiment ${\mathcal E}^\star_{1,n}$

nodes.name: Solve the volatility ODE between grid points
nodes.statement: Fix $\theta=(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in[0,\infty)^4$ with $\alpha\neq 0$. By solving the linear ODE for $h_{1,n}$ in (\ref{G1p}), observe that \begin{equation} h_{1,n}(t) = \frac\beta{\alpha} \bigl[1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha[t-(k - 1)/n]} \bigr]+ \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha[t-(k - 1)/n]} h_{1,n} \biggl(\frac{k-1} n \biggr)\vadjust{\goodbreak} \end{equation} for $(k - 1)/n\le t<k/n$, $1\le k\le n$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$. It thus follows from (\ref{specialHn1}) and (\ref{ode}) that for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$, \begin{eqnarray*} h_{1,n}(1/n-)&=&h_0\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha/n}+\frac{\beta}{\alpha}[1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha/n}] = h_{0,n}(\theta),\\ h_{1,n} \biggl(\frac k n- \biggr)&=&\beta_n(\theta)+ h_{1,n} \biggl(\frac{k - 1} n- \biggr) [\alpha_n(\theta)+\lambda_n(\theta) Z_{n,k-1}^2 ],\qquad 2\le k\le n. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Solve the volatility ODE between grid points

nodes.name: Identify GARCH volatilities with grid values; laws agree
nodes.statement: In view of (\ref{G1}) and the identities in the last display, we thus have $h_{n}(k)=h_{1,n} (((k + 1)/n)- )$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $0 \le k\le n - 1$ and $\theta=(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in[0,\infty)^4$ with $\alpha >0$. A similar argument is applicable to (\ref{specialHn2}) and $\theta=(h_0,\beta,0,\lambda)\in[0,\infty)^4$. It thus follows from (\ref{G1}) and (\ref{G1p}) that \[ {\mathcal L}_\theta \bigl(\bigl(G_{1,n}(k/n)\bigr)_{1\le k\le n} \bigr) = {\mathcal L}_\theta ((G_{n}(k))_{1\le k\le n} ),\qquad n\in\mathbb{N} , \theta\in[0,\infty)^4 . \]
nodes.statement_short: Identify GARCH volatilities with grid values; laws agree

nodes.name: Conclude ${\mathcal E}_{n,H^{(0)}_n}$ equivalent to ${\mathc
nodes.statement: Note that $G_{1,n}$ is constant on $[(k - 1)/n,k/n)$, $1 \le k \le n$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Hence, ${\mathcal E}_{n,H_n^{(0)}}$ is equivalent to ${\mathcal E}^{\star}_{1,n}$ in deficiency for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ by (\ref{defMarkov}) and the monotonicity theorem for\vspace*{1pt} Markov kernels (see~\cite{Re93}, Lemma 1.4.2(i)).
nodes.statement_short: Conclude ${\mathcal E}_{n,H^{(0)}_n}$ equivalent to ${\mathcal E}^\star_{1,n}$

nodes.name: Randomize the time grid: $V_{n,k}$ and $N_{2,n}$
nodes.statement: Next, we randomize the deterministic time grid. Therefore, let $(U_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ be an i.i.d. sequence of random variables independent of the vector $Z_n$, where $U_k$ is uniformly distributed on $[0,1]$. Set \begin{equation} V_{n,k} = \bigl((k - 1) + U_k\bigr)/n,\qquad 1\le k\le n, \end{equation} and define a point process $ N_{2,n}$ by \begin{equation} N_{2,n}=\sum_{k=1}^n 1_{Z_{n,k}\neq0} \varepsilon_{(V_{n,k},Z_{n,k})},\qquad n\in\mathbb{N} . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Randomize the time grid: $V_{n,k}$ and $N_{2,n}$

nodes.name: Define randomized experiment ${\mathcal E}^\star_{2,n}$; Lem
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be as in (\ref{timechange}). For $n\in\mathbb{N}$, let ${\mathcal E}^{\star}_{2,n}=(D_1,{\mathcal D}_1,({\mathcal L}_{\theta}(G_{2,n}))_{\theta \in[0,\infty)^4})$, where for all\break $0\le t\le1$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\theta=(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in[0,\infty)^4$, $(G_{2,n},h_{2,n})$ is the pathwise unique solution of the following system of integral equations: \begin{eqnarray} \hspace*{-15pt}G_{2,n}(t)& = &\int_{[0,t]\times\mathbb{R}} h^{1/2}_{2,n}(s-)z N_{2,n}(\mathrm{d}s,\mathrm{d}z),\nonumber\\ [-8pt]\\ [-8pt] \hspace*{-15pt}h_{2,n}(t) & = & h_0+ \int_{[0,t]}\beta-\alpha h_{2,n}(s-)\,\mathrm{d}T_{N_{2,n}} (s) + \lambda\int_{[0,t]\times\mathbb{R}} h_{2,n}(s-)z^2 N_{2,n}(\mathrm{d}s,\mathrm{d}z).\nonumber \end{eqnarray} To proceed with the proof of Theorem \ref{th2}, we need the following lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Define randomized experiment ${\mathcal E}^\star_{2,n}$; Lemma 4.1 needed

nodes.name: Bound $\Delta(\widehat{\mathcal E},{\mathcal E}^\star_{2,n})
nodes.statement: Let $N$ be a Poisson measure with intensity measure $\gamma\ell \otimes Q$. It follows from (\ref{hatEEE}) and~(\ref{EEE3}) that there exists a family of deterministic Markov kernels $K_\theta\dvtx\mathbb{M}_1\times{\mathcal D}_1\to[0,1]$, indexed by $\theta\in[0,\infty)^4$, such that both ${\mathcal L}_\theta(G_{2,n})=K_\theta{\mathcal L}(N_{2,n})$ and ${\mathcal L}_\theta (\widehat G)=K_\theta{\mathcal L}(N)$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\theta\in\Theta$. Since we have assumed (\ref{lre}), the assertion of Lemma \ref{thinning} holds and we thus get from (\ref{deflecamsmallerTV}) and the monotonicity theorem for Markov kernels (see \cite{Re93}, Lemma 1.4.2(i)) that as $n\to\infty$, \[ \Delta(\widehat{\mathcal E},{\mathcal E}^{\star}_{2,n})\le\sup_{\theta\in [0,\infty)^4}\| {\mathcal L}_\theta(\widehat G)-{\mathcal L}_\theta(G_{2,n})\|\le \|{\mathcal L}(N)-{\mathcal L}(N_{2,n})\|\to0 . \]
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\Delta(\widehat{\mathcal E},{\mathcal E}^\star_{2,n})$ by Lemma 4.1 and Markov kernels

nodes.name: Reduce to equivalence of ${\mathcal E}^\star_{1,n}$ and ${\m
nodes.statement: Consequently, ${\mathcal E}^{\star}_{2,n}$ converges (strongly) to $\widehat{\mathcal E}$ in deficiency as $n\to\infty$. Recall that ${\mathcal E}_{n,H_n^{(0)}}$ is equivalent to ${\mathcal E}_{1,n}^{\star}$ in deficiency for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$. To complete the proof of the theorem, it thus suffices to show that ${\mathcal E}^{\star}_{1,n}$ is equivalent to ${\mathcal E}^{\star}_{2,n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to equivalence of ${\mathcal E}^\star_{1,n}$ and ${\mathcal E}^\star_{2,n}$

nodes.name: Define time-change maps $T_{1..4,\sigma}$
nodes.statement: Therefore, let $\mathbb{M}_0$ denote the space of all non-negative point measures on $[0,1]$ with finite support. We equip this space with the $\sigma$-algebra ${\mathcal M}_0$ generated by point evaluations (see Reiss~\cite{Re93}, pages 5--6). Let $\mathbb{M}_{0,1}\subseteq\mathbb{M}_0$ be the subset of point measures $\sigma\in\mathbb{M}_0$ such that there exist $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and $0 = t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_{m} < 1$ with $\sigma=\sum_{k=1}^m\varepsilon_{t_k}$. For $\sigma\in\mathbb{M}_0$, we define mappings $T_{1,\sigma},T_{2,\sigma}\dvtx[0,1]\to[0,\infty)$ and $T_{3,\sigma},T_{4,\sigma}\dvtx[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R} $ as follows: if $\sigma\in\mathbb{M}_{0}\backslash\mathbb{M}_{0,1}$, then for all $t\in[0,1]$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}$, we set $T_{1,\sigma}(t)=T_{2,\sigma}(t)=t$ and $T_{3,\sigma}(t,x)=T_{4,\sigma}(t,x)=(t,x)$. Otherwise, if $\sigma\in\mathbb{M}_{0,1}$, then there exist $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and $0 = t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_{m} < 1$ with $\sigma=\sum_{k=1}^m\varepsilon_{t_k}$ and we set \begin{eqnarray*} T_{1,\sigma}(t)&=& \frac{t-t_k}{m(t_k-t_{k - 1})}+\frac km ,\qquad t\in[t_{k-1},t_k),\ 1\le k\le m ,\\ \nonumber T_{1,\sigma}(t)&=&\frac{t-t_m}{m(t_m-t_{m - 1})}+ 1 ,\qquad t\in[t_{m},1] . \end{eqnarray*} In this case, we define $T_{4,\sigma}\dvtx[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]\times \mathbb{R}$ by $T_{4,\sigma}=(T_{1,\sigma}(t),x)$. Then, $T_{1,\sigma}\dvtx[0,t_m]\to[0,1]$ and $T_{4,\sigma}\dvtx[0,t_m]\times\mathbb{R}\to[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}$ are bijections and we let $T_{2,\sigma}\dvtx[0,1]\to[0,t_m]$ and $T_{3,\sigma}\dvtx[0,1]\times \mathbb{R}\to[0,t_m]\times\mathbb{R}$ be their corresponding inverses.
nodes.statement_short: Define time-change maps $T_{1..4,\sigma}$

nodes.name: Define $M_{i,n}$ and time-changed equations
nodes.statement:
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Recall (ef{defVnk}) and set  egin{eqnarray*} M_{1,n}&=&\sum_{k=1}^n \varepsilon_{V_{n,k}} 1_{G_{1,n}(k/n)-G_{1,n}((k - 1)/n)
eq 0} ,\ M_{2,n}&=&\sum_{0\le t\le1} \varepsilon_{([tn]+1)/n} 1_{G_{2,n}(t)-G_{2,n}(t-)
eq0} . \end{eqnarray*} For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $i=1,2$, it follows from the transformation theorem that  egin{eqnarray} G_{i,n}\circ T_{i,M_{i,n}}(t)&=&\int_{[0,t]	imes\mathbb{R}} (h_{n,i}\circ T_{M_{i,n}})^{1/2}(s-) z N_{i,n}^{T_{i+2,M_{i,n}}}(\mathrm{d}s,\mathrm{d}z),
onumber \ h_{i,n}\circ T_{i,M_{i,n}}(t)&=&h_0 + \int_{[0,t]}  eta - \alpha (h_{i,n}\circ T_{i,M_{i,n}})(s-)\,\mathrm{d}T_{i,M_{i,n}}(s)\ &&{} + \lambda\int_{[0,t]	imes\mathbb{R}} (h_{i,n}\circ T_{i,M_{i,n}})(s-) z^2 N_n^{ T_{i+2,M_{i,n}}}(\mathrm{d}s,\mathrm{d}z)
onumber \end{eqnarray} for all $t\in[0,1]$ and $	heta=(h_0, eta,\alpha,\gamma)\in[0,\infty)^4$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $M_{i,n}$ and time-changed equations

nodes.name: Case $h_0=\beta=0$: both laws degenerate
nodes.statement: Let $\theta=(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\gamma)\in[0,\infty)^4$. If $h_0 = \beta = 0$, then it follows from (\ref{G1p}), (\ref{EEE3}) and (\ref{timechange1}) that $h_{i,n}=h_{i,n}\circ T_{i,M_{i,n}}\equiv 0$, $i=1,2$, a.s. and thus \[ {\mathcal L}_\theta(G_{i,n}) = {\mathcal L}_{\theta}(G_{i,n}\circ T_{i,M_{i,n}}) = \varepsilon_0,\qquad n\in\mathbb{N} , i=1,2 . \]
nodes.statement_short: Case $h_0=\beta=0$: both laws degenerate

nodes.name: Case $h_0+\beta>0$: time changes give mutual Markov kernels;
nodes.statement: Otherwise, if $h_0+\beta>0$, it follows from (\ref{G1p}) and (\ref{EEE3}) that $h_{i,n}(t)>0$ for all $t\in(0,1]$ a.s., $i=1,2$. In this case, we have $M_{1,n} = N_{2,n}$, $M_{2,n} = N_{1,n}$, $N_{1,n}^{T_{3,M_{1,n}}} = N_{n,2}$ and $N_{2,n}^{T_{4,M_{2,n}}} = N_{n,1}$ and thus we get from (\ref{timechange1}) that both \[ {\mathcal L}_\theta(G_{1,n}) = {\mathcal L}_{\theta}(G_{2,n}\circ T_{2,M_{2,n}}) \quad\mbox{and}\quad {\mathcal L}_\theta(G_{2,n})={\mathcal L}_{\theta}(G_{1,n}\circ T_{1,M_{1,n}}) \] for $n\in\mathbb{N}$. In other words, for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, there are Markov kernels $K_{1,2,n}\dvtx D_1\times{\mathcal D}_1\to[0,1]$ and $K_{2,1,n}\dvtx D_1\times{\mathcal D} _1\to [0,1]$, not depending on $\theta\in[0,\infty)^4$, such that $K_{1,2,n}{\mathcal L}_\theta(G_{2,n})={\mathcal L}_\theta(G_{1,n})$ and $K_{2,1,n}{\mathcal L}_\theta(G_{1,n}) = {\mathcal L}_\theta(G_{2,n})$ for all $\theta\in[0,\infty)^4$. Hence,~${\mathcal E}_{1,n}^{\star}$ is equivalent to~${\mathcal E}_{2,n}^{\star}$ in deficiency by (\ref{defMarkov}) for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$. This completes the proof of the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Case $h_0+\beta>0$: time changes give mutual Markov kernels; conclude

nodes.name: Reduce to the uniform TV bound (th2astronger) via Theorem 2.
nodes.statement: Recall that Le Cam's distance is a pseudo-metric. In view of (\ref{deflecamsmallerTV}) and Theorem \ref{th2}, it thus suffices to show (\ref{th2astronger}). For $n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $Z_n=(Z_{n,k})_{1\le k\le n}$ be a random vector with a~distribution as in (\ref{Znthinn}).
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the uniform TV bound (th2astronger) via Theorem 2.1

nodes.name: First assume $Q_n=Q$
nodes.statement: First, we assume that \begin{equation} Q_n = Q ,\qquad n\in\mathbb{N} . \end{equation} At the end of the proof we will relax this condition to $\|Q_n-Q\|\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: First assume $Q_n=Q$

nodes.name: Introduce $N_n$ and the two parametrizations $H_{1,n},H_{2,n
nodes.statement: Let $N_n$ be as in (\ref{defNn}) and set $\|N_n\|=N_n([0,1]\times \mathbb{R})$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Let $\Theta$ be as in the assertion of the theorem. Suppose that $H_{1,n}=H_n=(h_{0,1,n},\beta_{1,n},\alpha_{1,n},\lambda _{1,n})\dvtx\Theta\to[0,\infty)^4 $ satisfies the assumptions of the theorem. Further, let $H_{2,n}=(h_{0,2,n},\beta_{2,n},\alpha_{2,n},\lambda _{2,n})=H_{n}^{(0)}\dvtx\Theta\to[0,\infty)^4 $ be defined by the identities in (\ref{specialHn1}) and (\ref{specialHn2}).
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $N_n$ and the two parametrizations $H_{1,n},H_{2,n}$

nodes.name: Define GARCH processes $X_{i,n}$ and index set $M_{n,k}$
nodes.statement: For $\theta\in\Theta$ and $i=1,2$, we define $X_{i,n}=(X_{i,n}(k))_{1\le k\le n}$ by \begin{eqnarray} X_{i,n}(k)&=&h^{1/2}_{i,n}(k - 1) Z_{n,k},\qquad X_{i,n}(0)=0 ,\nonumber\\ h_{i,n}(k)&=&\beta_{i,n}(\theta)+ h_{i,n}(k - 1) [\alpha_{i,n}(\theta)+\lambda_{i,n}(\theta) Z_{n,k}^2 ] ,\\ h_{i,n}(0)&=&h_{0,i,n}(\theta) ,\qquad n\in\mathbb{N} , 1 \le k \le n .\nonumber \end{eqnarray} Hence, $X_{1,n}$ corresponds to the GARCH processes $G_n$ as in the theorem, and $X_{2,n}$ to the GARCH processes $G_n^{(0)}$ defined directly after (\ref{specialHn2}). Let \begin{equation} M_{n,k} = \Biggl\{\sigma=(\sigma _l)_{1\le l\le k}\in\mathbb{N}^k \dvtx \sum_{l=1}^k\sigma_l\le n \Biggr\},\qquad 1 \le k \le n , n\in\mathbb{N}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Define GARCH processes $X_{i,n}$ and index set $M_{n,k}$

nodes.name: Define coefficients $\eta$ and functions $\hat g$
nodes.statement:
By employing the conventions $0^0=1$ and $\sum_{l=k}^m=0$ for $m < k$, we set  egin{eqnarray} \eta_{i,n,1,l,\sigma}(	heta)&=& eta_{i,n}(	heta)\sum _{m=0}^{\sigma_{l + 1} - 1}[\alpha_{i,n}(	heta)]^m ,
onumber\ \eta_{i,n,2,l,\sigma}(	heta)&=&[\alpha_{i,n}(	heta)]^{\sigma _{l + 1}} ,\ \eta_{i,n,3,l,\sigma}(	heta)&=&\lambda_{i,n}(	heta) [\alpha _{i,n}(	heta)]^{\sigma_{l + 1} - 1}
onumber \end{eqnarray} for $\sigma=(\sigma_l)_{1\le l\le k}\in M_{n,k}$, $1 \le k \le n$, $0 \le l \le k - 1$, $i=1,2$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Also, we recursively define functions from $\mathbb{R}^k	o\mathbb{R}$ by setting  egin{eqnarray} \hat g_{i,n,0,\sigma,	heta}&\equiv&h_{0,i,n}(	heta) \alpha _{i,n}(	heta)^{\sigma_1-1}+ eta_{i,n}(	heta) \sum_{m=0}^{\sigma_1-2}\alpha_{i,n}^m(	heta) ,
onumber\ [-8pt]\ [-8pt] \hat g_{i,n,l,\sigma,	heta}(y)&=&\eta_{i,n,1,l,\sigma}(	heta)+\eta _{i,n,2,l,\sigma}(	heta) \hat g_{i,n,l - 1,\sigma,	heta}(y)+\eta_{i,n,3,l,\sigma}(	heta) y_l^2
onumber \end{eqnarray} for $y\in\mathbb{R}^k$, $\sigma=(\sigma_l)_{1\le l\le k}\in M_{n,k}$, $1 \le k \le n$, $0 \le l \le k - 1$, $i=1,2$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define coefficients $\eta$ and functions $\hat g$

nodes.name: Introduce jump stopping times $\tau_m$ and gaps $\Delta\tau$
nodes.statement_short: Introduce jump stopping times $\tau_m$ and gaps $\Delta\tau$

nodes.name: Define embedded process $Y_{i,n}$ and its recursion
nodes.statement:
Let $i=1,2$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $1 \le k \le n$ and $	heta\in \Theta$. On $\{\|N_n\|=0\},$ set $Y_{i,n}=0$, and otherwise,  egin{equation} Y_{i,n} = (Y_{i,n}(l))_{1\le l\le\|N_n\|} = (X_{i,n}(	au _l))_{1\le l\le\|N_n\|} . \end{equation} In the notation of (ef{defhateta}) and (ef{defhatg}), $Y_{i,n}$ satisfies the following recursion on $\{\|N_n\|=k\}$:  egin{eqnarray} Y_{i,n}(l) & = & g^{1/2}_{i,n}(l - 1) Z_{n,	au_l} ,\qquad Y_{i,n}(0) = 0 ,\qquad 1 \le l \le k ,
onumber \ g_{i,n}(l) & = & \eta_{i,n,1,l,\Delta	au}(	heta)+ g_{i,n}(l - 1) \eta_{i,n,2,l,\Delta	au}(	heta)
onumber\ [-8pt]\ [-8pt] &&{} +\eta_{i,n,3,l,\Delta	au}(	heta) g_{i,n}(l - 1) Z_{n,	au_l}^2 ,\qquad 1 \le l \le k - 1 ,
onumber \ g_{i,n}(0)&=&\hat g_{i,n,0,\Delta	au,	heta} .
onumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Define embedded process $Y_{i,n}$ and its recursion

nodes.name: Define events $A_{n,k,\sigma}$
nodes.statement: Recall (\ref{defMnk}). For all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $1 \le k \le n$ and $\sigma=(\sigma_l)_{1\le l\le k}\in M_{n,k}$, let \begin{equation} A_{n,k,\sigma} = \{ \|N_n\| = k , \Delta\tau = \sigma \} . \end{equation} For future purposes, we collect some useful inequalities in the next lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Define events $A_{n,k,\sigma}$

nodes.name: Uniform control of $\alpha_{i,n}^n$
nodes.statement: Let $(\Theta,(H_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}})$ be as in Theorem \ref{th2a}. First, note that $(\Theta,(H_{1,n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}})=(\Theta,(H_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}})$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem \ref{th2a}. Also, recall that $(\Theta,(H_{2,n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}})=(\Theta,(H^{(0)}_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}})$ is defined in (\ref{specialHn1}) and (\ref{specialHn2}). In particular, observe that $\alpha_{i,n}(\theta)\to1$ uniformly for all $\theta=(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in\Theta$ as $n\to\infty$, $i=1,2$, and thus there is an $n_1=n_1(\Theta)\in\mathbb{N}$ satisfying \begin{equation} \frac{\mathrm{e}^{-1}}2 \le[\alpha _{i,n}(\theta)]^n=\exp\bigl(n\log\bigl[n+n\bigl(\alpha_{i,n}(\theta) - 1\bigr)\bigr]-n\log n\bigr) \le 2 \mathrm{e} \end{equation} for all $n\ge n_1$, $i=1,2$ and $\theta=(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in\Theta$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniform control of $\alpha_{i,n}^n$

nodes.name: Lower and upper bounds on coefficients and $\hat g$
nodes.statement_short: Lower and upper bounds on coefficients and $\hat g$

nodes.name: Bounds on $\eta$ and their differences
nodes.statement:
Recall (ef{defhateta}) and (ef{defhatg}). It follows from (ef{upperbound}) that we have  egin{eqnarray} \max \{\eta_{i,n,2,l,\sigma}(	heta) , \eta_{i,n,3,l,\sigma}(	heta) \}&\le& C_1^2 ,
onumber\[2pt] \max \{\eta_{i,n,1,l,\sigma}(	heta) , \hat g_{i,n,0,\sigma,	heta} \}&\le& (k + 1) C_1^2 ,
onumber\[2pt] \max \{|[\alpha_{1,n}(	heta)]^m-[\alpha _{1,n}(	heta)]^m| \}&\le&  rac{C_1^2m} n ,\[2pt] \max \{|\eta_{1,n,j,l,\sigma}(	heta)-\eta _{2,n,j,l,\sigma}(	heta)| \dvtx j=1,2,3 \}&\le&  rac{(2\mathrm{e}^2 C_1^3)^k}n ,
onumber\[2pt] |\hat g_{1,n,0,\sigma,	heta}-\hat g_{2,n,0,\sigma,	heta}|&\le& rac{(4 \mathrm{e}^2 C_1^3)^k}n
onumber \end{eqnarray} for all $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$, $0 \le l\le k - 1$, $\sigma=(\sigma_l)_{1\le l\le k}\in M_{n,k}$, $i=1,2$, $m\in\mathbb{N}_0$ and $	heta\in\Theta$.
nodes.statement_short: Bounds on $\eta$ and their differences

nodes.name: Induction bounds conditional moments of $g_{i,n}$ and $Y_{i,
nodes.statement: Recall (\ref{Yip}). Let $S>1$ be such that $Q([-S,S])=1$ and set $C_2=C_2(S,\theta)=\mathrm{e}^2(1+S)^2C_1^4$ and $C_3=C_3(S,\theta)=S^2C_2$. It follows from an induction and the inequalities in~(\ref{upperbound2}) that \begin{eqnarray} E_\theta[g_{i,n}(l)|A_{n,k,\sigma}] &\le&C_1^2(k + 1) + C_1^2(1 + S^2)E_\theta[g_{i,n}(l - 1)|A_{n,k,\sigma}]\nonumber \\ [-10pt]\\ [-10pt] &\le&(k + 1)\sum_{m=0}^l (1 + S^2)^m C_1^{2(1+m)}\le C_2^k\nonumber \end{eqnarray} and thus that \begin{equation} E_\theta[Y^2_{i,n}(l)|A_{n,k,\sigma}] \le C_3^k \end{equation} for all $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$, $0 \le l \le k - 1$, $\sigma=(\sigma_l)_{1\le l\le k}\in M_{n,k}$, $i=1,2$ and $\theta\in\Theta$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction bounds conditional moments of $g_{i,n}$ and $Y_{i,n}$

nodes.name: Induction gives the conditional mean difference bound
nodes.statement: Finally, let $C=C(S,\theta)=12 \mathrm{e}^3 C_1^3C_3$. By an induction, it follows from (\ref{upperbound2})--(\ref{upperbound4})~that \begin{eqnarray*} &&E_\theta [ |\hat g_{1,n,l,\sigma,\theta}(Y_{1,n})- \hat g_{2,n,l,\sigma,\theta}(Y_{1,n}) | |A_{n,k,\sigma} ] \\[-2pt] &&\quad\le C^k_3\sum_{j=1}^3|\eta_{1,n,j,l}(\theta)-\eta _{2,n,j,l}(\theta)| + E_\theta [ |\hat g_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(Y_{1,n})- \hat g_{2,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(Y_{1,n}) | |A_{n,k,\sigma} ]\\[-2pt] &&\quad\le |\hat g_{1,n,0,\sigma,\theta}- \hat g_{2,n,0,\sigma,\theta} |+C^k_4\sum_{l=1}^{k-1}\sum _{j=1}^3|\eta_{1,n,j,l}(\theta)-\eta_{2,n,j,l}(\theta)| \le \frac{C^k}n \end{eqnarray*} for all $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$, $0 \le l \le k - 1$, $\sigma=(\sigma_l)_{1\le l\le k}\in M_{n,k}$ and $\theta\in\Theta$. This completes the proof in view of (\ref{lowerbound}) and (\ref{upperbound2}).
nodes.statement_short: Induction gives the conditional mean difference bound

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 5.1 for compactly supported $f$
nodes.statement: By assumption, we have $f(x)=0$ for all $|x|\ge S$ and some $S>0$. Hence, there are $n_0=n_0(f,\theta)\in\mathbb{N}$ and $C_1=C_1(f,\theta)\in(1,\infty)$ such that for $C$ replaced by $C_1$, the assertion of Lemma \ref{Lemexpectbound} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 5.1 for compactly supported $f$

nodes.name: Define diffeomorphisms $\Psi$ and densities $\tilde f$
nodes.statement: Let $n\ge n_0$, $i=1,2$, $\theta\in\Theta$, $1 \le k \le n$ and $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$. Recall (\ref{defhatg}). In view of (\ref{awayfromzero}), $\Psi_{i,n,\theta}\dvtx\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}^k$ is a\vadjust{\goodbreak} well defined $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism, where $\Psi_{i,n,\sigma,\theta}=(\psi_{i,n,l,\sigma,\theta})_{1\le l\le k}\dvtx\break\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}^k$ is defined by \begin{eqnarray} \psi_{i,n,l,\sigma,\theta}(y)=\frac{y_l}{\hat g^{1/2}_{i,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)} \end{eqnarray} for $y=(y_1,\dots,y_k)\in\mathbb{R}^k$ and $1\le l\le k$. For all $n\ge n_0$, $\theta\in\Theta$, $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$ and $\sigma \in M_{n,k}$, we define \[ \tilde f_{i,n,k,\sigma,\theta}(y) = \prod_{l=1}^k \frac{f(\psi_{i,n,l,\sigma,\theta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{i,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)},\qquad y\in\mathbb{R}^k , i=1,2 . \]
nodes.statement_short: Define diffeomorphisms $\Psi$ and densities $\tilde f$

nodes.name: Express conditional TV as $L^1$ distance of densities
nodes.statement: It follows from (\ref{defhatg}), (\ref{Yip}) and (\ref{Phiip}) that $\tilde f_{i,n,k,\sigma,\theta}$ is a density of the probability measure ${\mathcal L}_\theta (Y_{i,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} )$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure $\ell^{\otimes k}$ on ${\mathcal B}(\mathbb{R}^k)$. In particular, we must have \begin{equation} \bigl\|{\mathcal L}_\theta (Y_{1,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} ) -{\mathcal L}_\theta (Y_{2,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} ) \bigr\| = \frac 12\int_{\mathbb{R}^k}|\tilde f_{1,n,k,\sigma,\theta}(y)-\tilde f_{2,n,k,\sigma,\theta}(y)|\,\mathrm{d}y \end{equation} for all $\theta\in\Theta$, $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$ and $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Express conditional TV as $L^1$ distance of densities

nodes.name: Lipschitz bound on one-coordinate TV
nodes.statement: Suppose that $C_f\in(0,\infty)$ is a global Lipschitz constant of $f$. By means of simple substitutions, for all $\epsilon>0$ and $w, v\ge\epsilon$, we can observe that \[ \frac 12 \int \biggl|\frac{f(x/v)}{v}-\frac{f(x/w)}{w} \biggr|\,\mathrm{d}x \le \frac1 \epsilon (S^2 C_f+1) |v-w| . \] Consequently, for all $\epsilon>0$, we find a $\kappa_1=\kappa_1(f,\epsilon)\in(1,\infty)$ such that \[ \frac12 \int \biggl|\frac{f(x/v)}{v}-\frac{f(x/w)}{w} \biggr|\,\mathrm{d}x \le \kappa_1(\epsilon)|v-w|,\qquad v,w\ge\epsilon . \] In view of (\ref{awayfromzero}), there thus exists some $\kappa_2=\kappa_2(f,\Theta)\in(1,\infty)$ such that \begin{eqnarray} &&\frac12 \int \biggl|\frac{f(y_l/\hat g^{1/2}_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y))}{\hat g_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}^{1/2}(y)}- \frac{f(y_l/\hat g^{1/2}_{2,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{2,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)} \biggr|\,\mathrm{d}y_l\nonumber\\ [-8pt]\\ [-8pt] &&\quad\le\kappa_2|\hat g_{1,n,{l - 1},\sigma,\theta}(y)-\hat g_{2,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)|\nonumber \end{eqnarray} for all $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$, $1 \le l\le k$, $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$, $y\in\mathbb{R}^{k}$ and $\theta\in\Theta$.
nodes.statement_short: Lipschitz bound on one-coordinate TV

nodes.name: Integrate out last coordinate for a recursive bound
nodes.statement: By integrating over $y_k$, we get from (\ref{cinproof}) that \begin{eqnarray} &&\frac12\int_{\mathbb{R}^k}|\tilde f_{1,n,k,\sigma,\theta}(y)-\tilde f_{2,n,k,\sigma,\theta}(y)|\,\mathrm{d}y\nonumber\\ &&\quad\le \kappa_2\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k - 1}}\prod_{l=1}^{k-1} \frac{f(\psi_{1,n,l,\sigma,\theta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)} |\hat g_{1,n,k - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)- \hat g_{2,n,k - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y) |\,\mathrm{d}y\\ &&\qquad{} +\frac12\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k - 1}} \Biggl|\prod_{l=1}^{k-1} \frac{f(\psi_{1,n,l,\sigma,\theta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)}- \prod_{l=1}^{k-1} \frac{f(\psi_{2,n,l,\sigma,\theta}(y))}{\hat g^{1/2}_{2,n,l - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)} \Biggr|\,\mathrm{d}y\nonumber \end{eqnarray} for all $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$, $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$ and $\theta\in\Theta$.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate out last coordinate for a recursive bound

nodes.name: Bound remainder via Lemma 5.1
nodes.statement: It follows from (\ref{hatcondEgdiff}) that \begin{eqnarray} && \int_{\mathbb{R}^{k - 1}}\prod_{l=1}^{k-1} \frac{f(\psi_{1,n,l,\sigma,\theta}(y))}{g^{1/2}_{1,n,l - 1,\sigma ,\theta}(y)} |\hat g_{1,n,k - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y)- \hat g_{2,n,k - 1,\sigma,\theta}(y) |\,\mathrm{d}y\nonumber\\ [-8pt]\\ [-8pt] &&\quad=E_\theta [ |\hat g_{1,n,k - 1,\theta}(Y_{1,n})- \hat g_{2,n,k - 1,\theta}(Y_{1,n}) | |A_{n,k,\sigma}]\le \frac{C_1^k}n\nonumber \end{eqnarray} for all $n\ge n_0$, $1 \le k \le n$, $\sigma\in M_{n,k}$ and $\theta\in\Theta$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound remainder via Lemma 5.1

nodes.name: Conclude by induction over $k$
nodes.statement: Let $C=\mathrm{e} \kappa_2 C_1$. By induction, we thus get from (\ref{hatg0diff}) and (\ref{cinproof2})--(\ref{cinproof3}) that \[ \bigl \|{\mathcal L}_\theta (Y_{1,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} )-{\mathcal L} _\theta (Y_{2,n} |A_{n,k,\sigma} ) \bigr\| \le\frac{C^k}{n} , \] uniformly for all $n\,{\ge}\,n_0, 1\,{\le}\,k\,{\le}\,n, \sigma\,{\in}\,M_{n,k}$ and $\theta\,{\in}\,\Theta$. This completes the proof of the~lemma.\vspace*{-3pt}
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by induction over $k$

nodes.name: Approximate $f$ by Lipschitz compactly supported densities $
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a Lebesgue density of $Q$ and $\Theta$ be as in Theorem \ref{th2a}. We denote the positive part of a function $g\dvtx\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ by $g^+$. Let $C^\infty_C$ be the space of infinitely often continuously differentiable functions $g\dvtx\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ with compact support $\overline{\{g>0\}}$. As $C^\infty_C$ is dense in $L^1$, we find a sequence of $g_m\in C_C^\infty$, $m\in\mathbb{N}$, such that $\int|g_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell\to0$ as $m\to\infty$. It is immediate that both $\int|g_m^+-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell\to0$ and $\int g_m^+\,\mathrm{d}\ell\to1$ as $m\to \infty$. Without loss of generality, we may thus assume that $\int g_m^+\,\mathrm{d}\ell>0$ for all $m\in\mathbb{N}$. Then, $h_m:=g^+_m/\int g_m^+\,\mathrm{d}\ell$ defines a sequence of globally Lipschitz continuous probability densities with a compact support $\overline{\{h_m>0\}}$ such that $\int|h_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell\to0$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $f$ by Lipschitz compactly supported densities $h_m$

nodes.name: Define GARCH models with approximated noise
nodes.statement: For $m\in\mathbb{N}$, let $Z^{(m)}_n=(Z^{(m)}_{n,k})_{1\le k\le n}$ be a random vector with distribution \[ {\mathcal L}\bigl(Z^{(m)}_n\bigr)(B) = \biggl((1 - p_n)\varepsilon_0(B)+p_n \int _Bh_m\,\mathrm{d}\ell \biggr)^{\otimes n} , \] with $B\in{\mathcal B}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, $1\le k\le n$. If we replace $Z_{n,k}$ by $Z^{(m)}_{n,k}$ in (\ref{Xip}), then we get yet another family of GARCH models, $X^{(m)}_{i,n}=(X^{(m)}_{i,n}(k))_{1\le k\le n}$, say, indexed by $\theta\in\Theta$, $i=1,2$ and $m$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define GARCH models with approximated noise

nodes.name: Bound the effect of noise approximation in TV
nodes.statement: It follows from the monotonicity theorem for Markov kernels and a well-known upper bound for product measures (see \cite{Re93}, Lemma 1.4.2(i) and page 23) that for all \mbox{$i=1,2$}, \begin{eqnarray} \hspace*{-15pt}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\bigl\|{\mathcal L}_\theta(X_{i,n})-{\mathcal L} _\theta\bigl(X^{(m)}_{i,n}\bigr)\bigr\| &\le& \bigl\|{\mathcal L}(Z_{n})-{\mathcal L}\bigl(Z^{(m)}_n\bigr)\bigr\|\nonumber\\ [-8pt]\\ [-8pt] \hspace*{-15pt}&\le& n\bigl\|{\mathcal L}(Z_{n,1})-{\mathcal L}\bigl(Z^{(m)}_{n,1}\bigr)\bigr\|= \frac{n p_n}2 \int|h_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell .\nonumber \end{eqnarray}\looseness=0
nodes.statement_short: Bound the effect of noise approximation in TV

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 5.2 conditionally on jump patterns
nodes.statement: As $h_m$ is globally Lipschitz with a compact support $\overline{\{h_m>0\}}$ for all $m\in\mathbb{N}_0$, the assumptions of Lemma \ref{condTVlem} hold. For all $m\in\mathbb{N}$, there thus exist $n_m\in\mathbb{N}$ and $C_m=C(h_m,\Theta)\in(0,\infty)$ such that for all $n\ge n_m$, we get, by conditioning and the monotonicity theorem for Markov kernels, that \begin{equation} \sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\bigl\|{\mathcal L}_\theta \bigl(X^{(m)}_{1,n}\bigr)-{\mathcal L}_\theta\bigl(X^{(m)}_{2,n}\bigr)\bigr\| \le \frac 1n E \bigl[C_m^{\|N_n\|} \bigr] \end{equation} for $N_n$ as defined in (\ref{defNn}).
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 5.2 conditionally on jump patterns

nodes.name: Combine via triangle inequality; let $m\to\infty$
nodes.statement: Recall (\ref{Xip}). By combining (\ref{truncatednoise}) and (\ref{condTV1}), we get, from the triangle inequality, that \[ \sup_{\theta\in\Theta} \bigl\|{\mathcal L}_\theta(G_n)-{\mathcal L}_\theta \bigl(G_n^{(0)}\bigr) \bigr\| \le n p_n \int|h_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell+\frac1n E \bigl[C_m^{\|N_n\|} \bigr] \] for all $m\in\mathbb{N}$ and $n\ge n_m$. As (\ref{lre}) holds, we have $\lim_{n\to\infty}EC_m^{\|N_n\|}= e^{\lambda(C_m-1)}$ and thus \[ \limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta} \bigl\|{\mathcal L}_\theta (G_n)-{\mathcal L}_\theta\bigl(G_n^{(0)}\bigr) \bigr\| \le\lambda \limsup_{m\to\infty}\int|h_m-f|\,\mathrm{d}\ell=0 , \] giving (\ref{th2astronger}). This completes the proof of Theorem \ref{th2a} in the case where $Q_n=Q$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$ (see (\ref{QnequalsQ})).
nodes.statement_short: Combine via triangle inequality; let $m\to\infty$

nodes.name: Relax to $Q_n\to Q$ in total variation
nodes.statement: Now, assume that $Q_n\to Q$ in total variation norm as $n\to\infty$. For $m\in\mathbb{N}$, let $\widehat Z_n=(\widehat Z_{n,k})_{1\le k\le n}$ be a random vector with distribution \[ {\mathcal L}(\widehat Z_n) = \bigl((1 - p_n)\varepsilon_0+p_n Q_n \bigr)^{\otimes n},\qquad n\in\mathbb{N} . \] If we replace $Z_{n,k}$ by $\widehat Z_{n,k}$ in (\ref{Xip}), then we get the GARCH models in the assertion of the theorem. We denote them by $\widehat X_{i,n}$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $i=1,2$. By the same argument as in~(\ref{truncatednoise}), we must have, for all $i=1,2$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$ , \[ \sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\|{\mathcal L}_\theta(\widehat {X}_{i,n})-{\mathcal L}_\theta(X_{i,n})\| \le np_n\|Q_n-Q\| . \] As the right-hand side tends to zero, this completes the proof of the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Relax to $Q_n\to Q$ in total variation

nodes.name: Introduce i.i.d. innovations, uniforms and Poisson counts
nodes.statement: We first need to make some preparations. Let $Z=(Z_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ and $U=(U_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be independent sequences of i.i.d. random variables such that ${\mathcal L}(Z_1)=Q$ with Lebesgue density~$f$ and $U_1$ is uniformly distributed on $(0,1)$. For $d\in\mathbb{N}$, we denote the order statistics of $0,U_1,\ldots,U_d$ by $0=:U_{d,0}<U_{d,1}\le\cdots\le U_{d,d}$. For each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $\nu_n$ be a Poisson random variable with parameter $\gamma_n>0$, independent of $Z$ and $U$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce i.i.d. innovations, uniforms and Poisson counts

nodes.name: Represent $N$ and define jump increments
nodes.statement_short: Represent $N$ and define jump increments

nodes.name: Define sample space $\widetilde{\mathbb{R}}$
nodes.statement: Let $S_0=\mathbb{R}^0=\{0\}$ and $\widetilde\mathbb{R} = \bigcup_{d=0}^\infty\{d\} \times S_d\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$, where for $d\in\mathbb{N}$, $S_d$ equals the set of all $w=(w_1,\dots,w_d)'\in(0,1)^d$ such\vspace*{1pt} that $\sum_{i=1}^dw_i\le1$. We endow $S_d$ and $\widetilde\mathbb{R}$ with the Borel trace field ${\mathcal B}(S_d)$ ($d\ge0$) and the $\sigma$-algebra $\widetilde{\mathcal B}$, respectively, where $\widetilde{\mathcal B}$ is the set of all $B\subseteq\widetilde\mathbb{R}$ such that $B\cap(\{d\}\times S_d\times\mathbb{R}^{d})\in \{\varnothing,\{d\}\}\otimes{\mathcal B}(S_d)\otimes{\mathcal B}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ for all $d\in\mathbb{N}_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Define sample space $\widetilde{\mathbb{R}}$

nodes.name: Reduce to experiments ${\mathcal F}_n$, $\widehat{\mathcal F
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to experiments ${\mathcal F}_n$, $\widehat{\mathcal F}_n$ of observed jumps

nodes.name: Define diffeomorphism $\Psi$ via volatility recursions
nodes.statement:
Let $\widehat w_0=0$ and for $d>0$, set $\widehat w_d=(1/d,\dots,1/d)\in\mathbb{R}^d$. Recall that $\Theta\subseteq(0,\infty)	imes[0,\infty)^3$ and pick $d\in\mathbb{N}_0$, $	heta=(h_0, eta,\alpha,\lambda)\in\Theta$, $w=(w_1,\dots ,w_d)\in S_d\cup\{\widehat w_d\}$. We define a diffeomorphism $\Psi_{d,w,	heta}\dvtx\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}^d$ as follows: if $d=0$, then let $\Psi_{d,w,	heta}=0$; otherwise, if $d>0$,~let \[ \Psi_{d,w,	heta}(z)= (h_{d,w,	heta,k}^{1/2}(z) z_k )_{1\le k\le d},\qquad z=(z_1,\dots,z_d)\in\mathbb{R}^d , \] where for $2\le k\le d$, we recursively define  egin{eqnarray} h_{d,w,	heta,k}(z)&=& rac{ eta}{\alpha}(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha w_k})+ \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha w_k}(1+\lambda z_{k-1}^2) h_{d,w,	heta,k-1}(z) ,
onumber\ [-9pt]\ [-9pt] h_{d,w,	heta,1}(z)&\equiv&h_{d,w,	heta,1}= rac{ eta}{\alpha }(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha w_1})+ \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha w_1}h_{0},
onumber \end{eqnarray} provided $\alpha>0$ and otherwise, if $\alpha=0$, we set  egin{eqnarray} h_{d,	heta,w,k}(z)&=& eta w_k+ h_{d,	heta,w,k-1}(z)(1+\lambda z_{k-1}^2) ,
onumber \ [-9pt]\ [-9pt] h_{d,	heta,w,1}(z)&\equiv&h_{d,w,	heta,1}= eta w_1+ h_{0} .
onumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Define diffeomorphism $\Psi$ via volatility recursions

nodes.name: Define Hellinger integrals ${\mathcal H}$
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a strictly positive Lebesgue density of $Q$ and set \begin{eqnarray*} &&{\mathcal H}_{d,\theta_1,\theta_2,w}(\zeta) \\[-2pt] &&\quad= \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} ( |J_{\Psi^{-1}_{d,w,\theta _1}}(x)| f^{\otimes d}(\Psi^{-1}_{d,w,\theta_1}(x)) )^{ \zeta} ( |J_{\Psi^{-1}_{d,w,\theta_2}}(x)| f^{\otimes d}(\Psi^{-1}_{d,w,\theta_2}(x)) )^{ 1-\zeta}\,\mathrm{d}x \end{eqnarray*} for all $\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta$, $0 < \zeta < 1$, $w\in S_d\cup\{\widehat{w}_d\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define Hellinger integrals ${\mathcal H}$

nodes.name: Equivalence iff equal Hellinger transforms (Strasser)
nodes.statement: To summarize, we have thus far shown that for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, equivalence of ${\mathcal E}_{\gamma_n,Q}(\Theta)$ and $\widehat{\mathcal E}_{\gamma_n,Q}(\Theta)$ in deficiency\vadjust{\goodbreak} is equivalent to equivalence of ${\mathcal F}_{n}$ and $\widehat{\mathcal F}_{n}$ in deficiency. For the remaining part, recall that the two experiments are equivalent in deficiency if and only if their corresponding Hellinger transformations are equal (see \cite{St85}, Corollary 53.8). By solving the differential equations in (\ref{COG}) and (\ref{hatEEE}), we thus arrive at the following identity:\looseness=-1\vspace*{-1pt} \[ \sum_{d=1}^\infty\frac{\gamma_n^d\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma_n}}{d!} {\mathcal H}_{d,\theta_1,\theta_2,\widehat w_d}(\zeta) = \sum _{d=1}^\infty \frac{\gamma_n^d\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma_n}}{d!} \int_{S_d} {\mathcal H}_{d,\theta_1,\theta_2,w}(\zeta) \frac{\mathrm{d}w}{\ell ^{\otimes d}(S_d)}\vspace*{-2pt} \]\looseness=0 for all $\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta$, $0 < \zeta < 1$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Equivalence iff equal Hellinger transforms (Strasser)

nodes.name: Analyticity in $\gamma_n$ gives identity per $d$
nodes.statement: In the last display, the functions are analytical in $\gamma_n$; consequently, for all $d\in\mathbb{N}$, $\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta$, $0 < \zeta < 1$, we must have\vspace*{-1pt} \begin{equation} {\mathcal H}_{d,\theta_1,\theta_2,\widehat w_d}(\zeta) = \int_{S_d} {\mathcal H}_{d,\theta_1,\theta_2,w}(\zeta) \frac{\mathrm{d}w}{\ell ^{\otimes d}(S_d)}.\vspace*{-2pt} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Analyticity in $\gamma_n$ gives identity per $d$

nodes.name: Monotonicity of $h\mapsto g_{f,\zeta_0}(\sqrt h)$
nodes.statement: Next, we return to the proof of the theorem. By our assumption, there exists $\zeta_0\in(0,1)$ such that, with $g_{f,\zeta_0}\dvtx(0,\infty)\to[0,1]$ as in (\ref{defgQz}), $g_{f, \zeta_0}$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1]$. As a result, $h\mapsto g_{f, \zeta_0}(\sqrt{h})$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity of $h\mapsto g_{f,\zeta_0}(\sqrt h)$

nodes.name: Define $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$ and take $d=1$
nodes.statement: For all $\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta$, define $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}\dvtx(0,1]\to(0,\infty)$ by $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(w):=h_{1,w,\theta_2,1}(1)/h_{1,w,\theta_1,1}(1)$ for $0 < w \le 1$. In particular, taking $d=1$ and $\zeta=\zeta_0$ in (\ref{centralidentitynoneq}), we must have\vspace*{-1pt} \begin{equation} g_{f,\zeta_0} \bigl\{\sqrt{H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(1)} \bigr\} = \int_{(0,1)} g_{f,\zeta_0} \bigl\{\sqrt{H_{\theta_1,\theta _2}(w)} \bigr\}\,\mathrm{d}w\vspace*{-2pt} \end{equation} for all $\theta_1,\theta_2\in\Theta$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$ and take $d=1$

nodes.name: Parts (i),(ii): monotone $H$ contradicts identity
nodes.statement: (i) and (ii) For $i=1,2,$ let $\theta_i=(h_{0,i},\beta_i,\alpha,\lambda)\in\Theta$. Then,\vspace*{-1pt} \[ h^2_{1,w,\theta_1,1}(1) \mathrm{e}^{\alpha w} \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}w}H_{\theta _1,\theta_2}(w) = \beta_2 h_{0,1}-\beta_1 h_{0,2},\qquad 0< w\le 1 .\vspace*{-2pt} \] (Note that this formula extends to $\alpha=0$.) If $\beta_1 = \beta_2 > 0$ and $h_{0,1} > h_{0,2}$, then $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$ is strictly increasing with $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(1) \le1$, contradicting (\ref{centralidentitynoneq2}) since $h\mapsto g_{f, \zeta_0}(\sqrt{h})$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1]$. If $h_{0,1} = h_{0,2}$ and $\beta_2 < \beta_1$, then $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$ is strictly decreasing with $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(0+)=1$, contradicting (\ref{centralidentitynoneq2}) since $h\mapsto g_{f, \zeta_0}(\sqrt{h})$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1]$. Reversing the roles of parameters by replacing $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$ with $H_{\theta_2,\theta_1}$, the previous reasoning extends to the remaining cases where either $\beta_1 = \beta_2 > 0$ and $h_{0,1} < h_{0,2}$, or $h_{0,1} = h_{0,2}$ and $\beta_2 > \beta_1$. This completes the proof of (i) and (ii).
nodes.statement_short: Parts (i),(ii): monotone $H$ contradicts identity

nodes.name: Part (iii): $H=e^{(\alpha_1-\alpha_2)w}$
nodes.statement: (iii) If $(h_{0},\beta,\alpha_1,\lambda),(h_{0},\beta,\alpha_2,\lambda)\in \Theta$ and $\beta=0$, then we have $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(w)=\mathrm{e}^{(\alpha_1-\alpha_2)w}$ for all $w\in(0,1]$. (Note that this formula extends to $\alpha_1=0$ or $\alpha_2=0$.) By the same arguments as in parts (i) and (ii), we get from (\ref{centralidentitynoneq2}) that $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Part (iii): $H=e^{(\alpha_1-\alpha_2)w}$

nodes.name: Part (iv): contradiction from strict monotonicity
nodes.statement: (iv) In view of (iii), we may assume that $\beta>0$. Contradicting the hypothesis, we assume that $\alpha_2>0$. It follows from the strict inequality $\mathrm{e}^x-1>x$, $x>0$, that\vspace*{-1pt} \begin{eqnarray*} (h_0+\beta w)^2 \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}w}H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(w) &=&\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha_2w} \biggl\{w(\beta^2 - \alpha_2\beta h_0)-h_0^2\alpha_2 - \frac{\beta^2}{\alpha_2} (\mathrm{e}^{\alpha_2w} - 1) \biggr\}\\[-1pt] &<&-\alpha_2 h_0 \mathrm{e}^{-\alpha_2 w}(h_0+w\beta) < 0\vspace*{-2pt} \end{eqnarray*} for all $w\in(0,1]$. Thus, $w\mapsto H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(w)$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,1]$ with $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(0+)=1$, contradicting (\ref{centralidentitynoneq2}). Thus, we must have $\alpha_2=0$.\vadjust{\goodbreak}
nodes.statement_short: Part (iv): contradiction from strict monotonicity

nodes.name: Part (v): two cases on $h_0$
nodes.statement: (v) Let $(h_{0},\beta,\alpha_1,\lambda),(h_{0},\beta,\alpha_2,\lambda)\in \Theta$ with $\alpha_{2}>\alpha_{1}$. Without loss of generality, we may assume that $\beta > 0$. First, assume that $\beta/\alpha_2\le h_0\le \beta/\alpha_1$. Then, $\beta-\alpha_1 h_0\ge0$ and $\beta-\alpha_2 h_0\le0$. Note that we cannot simultaneously have that $\beta - \alpha_1 h_0=\beta - \alpha_2 h_0= 0$ such that \[ h_{1,w,\theta_1,1}^2 \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}w}H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(w) = (\beta - \alpha_2h_0)\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha_2 w}h_{1,w,\theta_1,1} -(\beta - \alpha_1h_0)\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha_1 w}h_{1,w,\theta_2,1}<0 \] for all $0<w\le1$. Consequently, $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$ is strictly decreasing with $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(0+)=1$, contradicting (\ref{centralidentitynoneq2}). Second, let $h_0<\beta/\alpha_2$ and set \[ \psi(w):= (\beta-\alpha_2h_0)h_{1,w,\theta_1,1} -(\beta-\alpha_1h_0)\mathrm{e}^{-(\alpha_1-\alpha_2) w}h_{1,w,\theta_2,1},\qquad 0<w\le1 . \] As we have $\alpha_2>\alpha_1$ and $h_0<\beta/\alpha_2$, we must have that $\beta - \alpha_1h_0>\beta - \alpha_2h_0>0$ such~that \[ \psi'(w)=(\alpha_1 - \alpha_2)(\beta - \alpha_1h_0)\mathrm{e}^{-(\alpha _1 - \alpha_2) w}h_{d,w,\theta_2,1}<0,\qquad 0<w\le1 . \] Note that $\psi(0+)=(\alpha_1 - \alpha_2) h_0^2<0$ and thus $\psi(w)<0$ for all $0<w\le1$. Since\break $\mathrm{e}^{\alpha_2w }h_{d,w,\theta_1,1}^2 \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}w}H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(w)=\psi(w)<0$ for all $0 < w \le 1$, $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$ is strictly decreasing with $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(0+)=1$, contradicting (\ref{centralidentitynoneq2}). This completes the proof of (v).
nodes.statement_short: Part (v): two cases on $h_0$

nodes.statement: (v) Let $(h_{0},\beta,\alpha_1,\lambda),(h_{0},\beta,\alpha_2,\lambda)\in \Theta$ with $\alpha_{2}>\alpha_{1}$. Without loss of generality, we may assume that $\beta > 0$.

Note that we cannot simultaneously have that $\beta - \alpha_1 h_0=\beta - \alpha_2 h_0= 0$ such that \[ h_{1,w,\theta_1,1}^2 \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}w}H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(w) = (\beta - \alpha_2h_0)\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha_2 w}h_{1,w,\theta_1,1} -(\beta - \alpha_1h_0)\mathrm{e}^{-\alpha_1 w}h_{1,w,\theta_2,1}<0 \] for all $0<w\le1$. nodes.name: Case $h_0<\beta/\alpha_2$: sign of $\psi$ gives contradictio
nodes.statement: Second, let $h_0<\beta/\alpha_2$ and set \[ \psi(w):= (\beta-\alpha_2h_0)h_{1,w,\theta_1,1} -(\beta-\alpha_1h_0)\mathrm{e}^{-(\alpha_1-\alpha_2) w}h_{1,w,\theta_2,1},\qquad 0<w\le1 . \] As we have $\alpha_2>\alpha_1$ and $h_0<\beta/\alpha_2$, we must have that $\beta - \alpha_1h_0>\beta - \alpha_2h_0>0$ such~that \[ \psi'(w)=(\alpha_1 - \alpha_2)(\beta - \alpha_1h_0)\mathrm{e}^{-(\alpha _1 - \alpha_2) w}h_{d,w,\theta_2,1}<0,\qquad 0<w\le1 . \] Note that $\psi(0+)=(\alpha_1 - \alpha_2) h_0^2<0$ and thus $\psi(w)<0$ for all $0<w\le1$. Since\break $\mathrm{e}^{\alpha_2w }h_{d,w,\theta_1,1}^2 \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}w}H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(w)=\psi(w)<0$ for all $0 < w \le 1$, $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}$ is strictly decreasing with $H_{\theta_1,\theta_2}(0+)=1$, contradicting (\ref{centralidentitynoneq2}). This completes the proof of (v).

nodes.statement: Next, we show that $\delta({\mathcal F},{\mathcal E}_h)=0$. To this end, we define $\xi=(\xi_1,\dots,\xi_3)\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\to[0,\infty)^3$ as follows. Let $\omega=(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_4)\in[0,\infty]^4$. If $(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_3)\in[0,\infty)^3$, then we set $\xi(\omega)=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3)$; if $\omega_1\in [0,\infty)$ and either $\omega_2=\infty$ or $\omega_3=\infty$, then we set $\xi(\omega)=(\omega_1,0,0)$; otherwise, we set $\xi(\omega)=0$.

eq y(1)$ and $y(1)

eq x(k - 1)\}\wedge1,\qquad (x,y)\in[\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}]^2 . \] Let $S_n$ be the set of all $(x,y)\in[\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}]^2$ with $3 \le T(x,y) \le n - 2$ such that $x(T)=x(T + 1)=x(T + 2)$. Consider the subset $M_{T,n}\subseteq S_n$ of all $(x,y)\in[\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}]^2$ such that both $y(T)

nodes.statement: For all $n\ge5$, we define a mapping $X_n\dvtx[\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}]^2\to[0,\infty]^4$ as follows: fix $(x,y)\in[\mathbb{R}^{n + 1}]^2$ and set $T=T_n(x,y)$. nodes.name: Part (ii): sufficiency and necessity
nodes.statement: (ii) First, assume that $\Theta$ satisfies (\ref{hsgleichbetaalphagleich}) for all $x>0$. Without loss of generality, we may assume that $\Theta\subseteq[0,\infty)^4$ is a finite set (see \cite{St85}, Theorem 51.4). Define $\Omega_\Theta$ to be the set of all $\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4) \in(0,\infty)\times\{\infty\}^2\times\{0,\infty\}$ such that $( \omega_1,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in(\Theta\cap\Theta_e)\backslash \widehat\Theta_e$ for some $(\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in[0,\infty)^3$. If $\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4)\in\Omega_\Theta$, then it follows from (\ref{hsgleichbetaalphagleich}) that the corresponding pair $(\beta,\alpha)=(\beta(\omega_1),\alpha(\omega_1))\in [0,\infty)^2$ is uniquely determined by $\omega_1$. Hence, we may define a mapping $Y\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\to[0,\infty]^4$ as follows: if $\omega=(\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3,\omega_4)\in\Omega_\Theta$, then we set $Y(\omega)=( \omega_1,\beta(\omega_1),\alpha(\omega_1),\omega_4)$; otherwise, if $\omega\in[0,\infty]^4\backslash\Omega_\Theta$, then we set $Y(\omega)=\omega$. As $\Theta$, and thus $\Omega_\Theta$, is a finite set, the mapping $Y$ is ${\mathcal B}([0,\infty]^4)/{\mathcal B}([0,\infty]^4)$-measurable. In view of (\ref{hsgleichbetaalphagleich}), note that $Q^Y_\theta=\widehat Q_\theta$ for all $\theta\in\Theta$ and thus $\delta({\mathcal F}(\Theta),\widehat{\mathcal F}(\Theta))=0$, by~(\ref{defMarkov}). Second, assume that (\ref{hsgleichbetaalphagleich}) is violated. There then exist some $h_0 > 0$, $\theta_1=(h_{0},\beta_1,\alpha_2,\lambda_1)$ $\in\Theta\cap\Theta_{e}\cap\widehat\Theta_{e}^C$ and $\theta_2=(h_{0},\beta_2,\alpha_2,\lambda_2)\in\Theta\cap\Theta_{e}$ such that $(\beta_1,\alpha_{1})\neq(\beta_2,\alpha_{2})$. Consider $\Theta_{0}=\{\theta_{1},\theta_{2}\}$ and the decision space $D=\{(\beta_1,\alpha_1),(\beta_2,\alpha_2)\}$, endowed with the discrete topology. For $\theta=(h_0,\beta,\alpha,\lambda)\in\Theta$, consider (continuous and bounded) loss functions $W_\theta\dvtx D\to\mathbb{R}$, where for $x=(x_1,\dots,x_4)\in[0,\infty]^4$, we set $W_{\theta}(x)=1-1_{\{(\beta,\alpha)\}}(x_2,x_3)$. Further, we define a Markov kernel $\widehat\rho\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\times{\mathcal B}(D)\to[0,1]$, where for $x\in[0,\infty]^4$ and $B\in{\mathcal B}(D)$, we set \[ \widehat\rho(x,B) = \cases{ \epsilon_{(\beta_1,\alpha_1)}(B) ,&\quad if $x\in(0,\infty)\times \{\beta_1\}\times\{\alpha_1\}\times[0,\infty)$,\cr \epsilon_{(\beta_2,\alpha_2)}(B) ,&\quad otherwise. } \] We then have $\int W_{\theta_i}(x) \widehat\rho(\omega,\mathrm{d}x) \widehat Q_{\theta_i}(\mathrm{d}\omega)=0$ for $i = 1,2$. On the other hand, any Markov kernel $\rho\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\times{\mathcal B}(D)\to[0,1]$ is of the form $\rho(\omega,B)=p(\omega)\epsilon_{(\beta_1,\alpha_1)}(B)+ (1-p(\omega))\epsilon_{(\beta_2,\alpha_2)}(B)$, where $p\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\to[0,1]$ is Borel, $\omega\in[0,\infty]^4$ and $B\in{\mathcal B}(D)$. It is easy to see that for such a Markov kernel $\rho$, there exists a Markov kernel $ \bar\rho\dvtx[0,\infty]^4\times {\mathcal B}(D)\to[0,1]$ such that both \[ \int W_{\theta_1}(x) \rho(\omega,\mathrm{d}x) Q_{\theta_1}(\mathrm{d}\omega)\ge \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma} \bigl(1-p(h_0,\infty,\infty,\infty)\bigr) \] and \[ \hspace*{-22pt}\int W_{\theta_2}(x) \rho(\omega,\mathrm{d}x) Q_{\theta_2}(\mathrm{d}\omega)\ge \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}p(h_0,\infty,\infty,\infty) . \] In view of (\ref{defdeffic}), we thus have $\delta({\mathcal F}(\Theta),\widehat{\mathcal F}(\Theta))\ge \delta({\mathcal F}(\Theta_0),{\mathcal F}(\Theta_0))\ge \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}/2$, which completes the proof of (ii).
